evidence.fact: Axon Draft One already writes draft incident reports from body-cam audio and saves roughly 40% of report-writing time. Officers still have to attest to each report, and it then goes through sergeant review and records review.

At Arvada PD, officers review, edit and finalize every AI-drafted report, and supervisors review and approve all submitted reports. The AI is treated as a support tool, and humans remain responsible for accuracy.

California SB 524 (Penal Code 13663, in effect since 1 January 2026) requires AI-assisted police reports to carry a disclosure and an officer's signature confirming the facts, and the first AI draft must be kept.

Existing AI returns agents check the order, test eligibility against written policy, work out the refund or store credit and update the order and payment systems. Policy exceptions are escalated to a human, so they still need human judgment.

Retail planning software already uses AI to split top-level open-to-buy budgets across product and location groups and to adjust replenishment automatically. Logile markets AI-built store labor budgets.

In-store refund and void approvals rely on manager overrides tied to named user accounts. Loss-prevention experts recommend a second approval for higher-value refunds. This is an internal control set by each retailer, not a legal or licensing requirement, and approvals can already be done remotely from a mobile device.

PackageX Mailroom says its AI and machine vision read package labels from a photo, match items to recipients, send email, SMS or WhatsApp alerts and record proof of pickup. This automates the logging and notification steps, though the claims come from the vendor's own materials.
The app lets staff batch-scan packages and notify all recipients with one tap. A person still has to physically receive, scan, sort and hand over the items.

Independent reviews mostly repeat the vendor's description. Vendors pitch self-service workflows as a way to reduce front-desk work, not as autonomous handling of physical mail, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Operto ONE runs seven AI agents across front-of-house and back-of-house hotel work. A supervisory layer decides whether each agent drafts, recommends or acts, depending on how confident it is. The agents coordinate tasks, but managers still oversee them.

Apaleo and THE FLAG run an agentic AI in live hotel operations that creates tasks for departments on its own, such as extra beds or cots. It saves about 3.5 hours a week of task creation. It routes and coordinates operational work but does not replace managers conferring with each other.

Sirma's Marta agent links to the PMS, revenue and operations systems. It updates plans and sends tasks to the right teams, which covers the information-sharing part of coordination. Decisions and negotiation between managers stay with humans.

AI needs-assessment generators can build a framework that pulls together census and demographic data, service utilization records, survey instruments and engagement strategies. They produce plans and templates, not finished analyses of the data.

A 2026 academic paper describes using AI for pattern detection, classification, prioritization and decision support on community-needs survey data to guide program planning. This shows the analysis sub-steps can be automated, though it is a research method rather than a deployed product.

Census figures are the standard population source for needs assessments but do not give an exact count of a community. Program needs assessments still rely on direct input from community members, which calls for human engagement and judgment to interpret.

Vendors sell purchase-order tracking agents. These agents read open PO records, supplier emails, receipts and invoices, label the status of each order and draft chase notes for a buyer to review. A human review step is still built in.
Dynamics 365 ERP MCP servers let AI agents reach live ERP purchasing and inventory data directly. Other vendor agents connect to SAP, Oracle and NetSuite and log every PO action for audit.

Supplier performance agents pull delivery, quality and cost data from ERP records and score suppliers against targets automatically. Vendors still stress human approval for important supplier decisions.

Vendor material describes ITAM, procurement and MDM pipelines (an HRIS trigger, then an asset request, then Jamf/Intune enrollment) that automate the digital side: reading orders, matching the hardware to the role, and setting up the device. Each new hire automatically triggers an asset request in the ITAM platform.

In zero-touch deployment, devices ship from the vendor already configured, which cuts down the technician's hands-on setup. Physical checks and handling still happen at the vendor or depot. The agent has no body, so it cannot look over the hardware itself.
IT provisioning and asset roles still involve hands-on prep and inspection of hardware before it is handed to users. No law or licence requires a human to sign off on this.

Oracle Autonomous Database and Data Safe already automate routine security work: security patching (Oracle says without downtime), encryption, user and security assessments, activity monitoring and data masking. Customers still have to classify their data and check that access policies match their rules.
Oracle says its autonomous database applies security patches automatically and encrypts network traffic automatically. Both claims come from Oracle's own materials.

Agents with database access can change permissions, and reported incidents include an agent running a destructive query on a production database. Guidance therefore calls for least-privilege access and human oversight, so a human still has to review and approve security changes before they are used.

Sketch-to-CAD and drawing-to-CAD AI tools in 2026 handle simple geometry from digital sketches or images. Complex parts still need human cleanup, and engineers review and approve the output. These tools help digitally but do not draw sketches by hand, trace onto paper or run copiers.

Turiya AI reads drawings supplied as images or PDFs and generates CAD code and 3D models. Engineers stay in control and review the results, so the tool supports digital reproduction steps rather than physical tracing or copying.
Drafter certification (ADDA Certified Drafter) is voluntary, and no general license is needed to draft, trace or reproduce drawings.
Library systems already let patrons pay fines online through PayPal or card. Payments post to the patron's account automatically, so collection needs no staff action.
Patrons can choose which fines to pay and pay part of a fine through self-service online portals.
Library chatbots answer routine fine and account questions. Judgment calls, such as disputes or waivers, still go to a human, and in-person cash payments at the desk need someone physically there.

Pharmacy inventory software already handles the main record-keeping steps. It automatically reconciles wholesaler invoices so staff don't have to match paper invoices against packing slips by hand, and it keeps purchase orders and inventory levels up to date. An agent working in the browser could run these screens from start to finish.

Pharmacy management systems update a running inventory count from electronic wholesaler data (EDI) and invoices, and can track stock by lot and expiry date. Most of the data entry is structured digital work that an agent can do.

For controlled substances, the buyer has to record how many containers actually arrived and the date they arrived. Someone has to physically count the delivery, and only an authorized registrant can sign Form 222 or use a CSOS certificate. This keeps a human involved for checking deliveries and for the controlled-substance steps, even though the aide's routine record entry doesn't require a licence.

Jail management systems already handle booking records, charges, bond and holds, and they auto-fill arrest and charge data from connected CAD/RMS or arrest-report systems. This automates much of the data entry and updating.
Arrest information can be pulled into the jail system to fill in cases, charges and bond details, and staff can update charges, court dates and inmate records in real time.

Identification needs in-person steps by corrections deputies: Live Scan fingerprinting, photos, and documenting scars and tattoos. Checking identity against NCIC and state databases happens inside restricted criminal-justice (CJIS) systems.

Machines that peel produce automatically, such as the Minerva Omega onion and potato peeler at up to 240 kg/h, are mechanical kitchen equipment. They are not software AI agents, so the reference technology, which has no body, cannot run or replace them.
Peeling machines sold to restaurants, like the Cancan 1323, still need a person to load, run and unload them. Washing, peeling, cutting and seeding produce all means handling it physically.

Commercial vegetable prep machines such as the IMC MF5 are electromechanical tools. The task is manual or machine-assisted work, so an agent that only uses software can do nothing meaningful here beyond things like recipe or cut-spec lookup.
Automated meat cutting depends on physical robots: a six-axis arm with 3-D machine vision is used to cut beef hocks in processing plants. That is industrial robotics, not a software agent.
Research systems that cut pork carcasses into primal cuts need fixtures, saws and robot arms. The task is physical manipulation of the meat.
Fully automatic primal cutting of pig half carcasses uses a vision-positioned saw. This is specialised hardware that a software-only agent cannot operate in a typical kitchen.

The robots that help with bussing (Bear Robotics Servi, Pizza Ranch units) are physical carts. Humans still load the dirty dishes, and the robots carry them to the dish room. That makes them robotics, not software agents, and they still don't wipe tables.
Even a purpose-built autonomous bussing robot (Smile Robotics) is much slower than a human at clearing tables. This shows the task depends on physical manipulation.
Restaurants deploy robots to carry dirty dishes to the dish room, which is entirely physical work. An agent that acts only through software has nothing to act on.
Caring for Our Children defines cleaning as physically removing dirt with soap, water and friction, then sanitizing surfaces. This is hands-on handling of objects.
Childcare guidance says mouthed and shared toys must be cleaned and sanitized at least daily or whenever soiled. Some guidance says after each use, with a separate bin for mouthed toys.
Sanitizers must be EPA-registered and used as the label says, including dilution and contact time. Licensing sets the standards but does not require a licensed person to do the cleaning.

ChatCPR is an open-source AI tool from UC San Diego, Johns Hopkins and UPMC. It talks bystanders through CPR and did better than human 911 dispatchers in early testing (May 2026). This is help to a human who does the CPR, not a replacement, so it supports L1 at most.
A test with 21 people used a voice chatbot to guide untrained users through CPR. Only 33% of them gave high-quality CPR. In every case a human had to do the chest compressions with their own hands.
Most states require child-care providers to hold first aid and CPR certification. This is a training rule for the caregiver, and it assumes a person on the spot gives the care by hand.

Camera and IoT baby monitors (for example CuboAi, and research prototypes such as ThermoCam) can watch a child and send fever or temperature alerts. They support observation, but they do not take a reading by hand, drive a child to the doctor or give medicine.

Under Texas HB 1615 (Nathan's Law), child-care staff need a parent's signed, electronic or phoned-in authorization before giving a child medication. The rule covers medication given through a parent's authorization; it does not require a licensed professional, so a lay caregiver can do it with consent.
Utah's child-care rules require parental consent each time over-the-counter medication is given. Giving medication is a physical, hands-on job done by the caregiver who is present.

Park and recreation departments already use AI to draft social media posts and program descriptions, and to suggest new programs from national trend data and local data. This covers the promote and organize sub-steps.

Rec Technologies sells recreation management software it calls AI-powered, with email and SMS program marketing and help with registration and administration. Its feature claims come from its own vendor pages.
Recreation workers plan and lead activities in person, supervise participants and keep them safe. Some employers require CPR or first aid certification, so the leading part needs physical presence.

Vendor pages say AI property-inquiry assistants answer buyer questions around the clock. They cover property details, HOA fees, taxes and mortgage estimates, and they qualify buyers on financing. These are marketing claims with no independent accuracy data.
A mortgage AI tool (Roof AI from Mortgageable) answers routine financing questions 24/7 and sends complex cases to human advisers. This supports partial delegation, not full delegation.

Agents who answer outside their expertise, such as repair costs, construction or inspections, face negligence claims and discipline. That gives a reason to have a human review answers, though no law says a human must give them. These sources are secondary.

Libraries now automate returns sorting with robotic materials handling: conveyors read each item's RFID tag and route it to bins. That is physical robotics, which is outside the reference agent's abilities.
Even with automated sorters, staff still carry materials to the shelves on carts and place them by hand. Shelving remains physical work.
Sorting is driven by RFID lookups in the library management system (SIP2). That digital step is small and already automated, and no law requires a human to do or sign this task.

Aurelian's AI voice assistant is used by more than a dozen 911 centers, including Snohomish County WA, Chattanooga and Kalamazoo. It handles non-emergency calls such as noise and parking complaints and transfers real emergencies to a human dispatcher.
In 2025 Dakota County, MN's AI attendant redirected about 33% of calls to the dispatch center and answered common questions. Anoka County, MN is launching an AI non-emergency call taker.

AI only rarely answers 911 calls directly. NENA's operations and standards VP said a caller reporting an emergency should hear a human voice. State rules such as Utah's require at least two telecommunicators answering 911 at all times.

The carrier Hirschbach uses Augment's AI agent, Augie, for outbound driver outreach: information requests and pickup and delivery arrivals. That is about 40% of its track-and-trace contacts. Humans still handle the rest.

Vendor voice AI agents (Bubba AI, Bland, Telnyx) say they handle check calls, status updates, dispatch instructions and rescheduling. They connect to TMS and ELD systems and pass exceptions to human dispatchers. These are the vendors' own unverified claims.

A third-party guide summarizing FCC rules says business and industrial two-way land mobile radio needs no commercial operator licence. I did not confirm this against current 47 CFR Part 90, so no legal rule appears to require a human operator.
O*NET lists this as a Machinists (51-4041.00) task. The neighbouring tasks are taking machines apart with hand or power tools and replacing defective parts, which is hands-on mechanical work.

Job postings describe installing machined replacement or repaired parts in mechanisms, machines and equipment, then running the unit to check that it works. All of this needs someone physically there. An agent with no body can only help at the edges, for example by finding manuals, torque specs or installation steps.
Machinists generally do not need a licence or sign-off for this work, so the main barrier is physical, not legal.

Driverless parking at SAE Level 4 depends on specially equipped vehicles and garage infrastructure, such as the Bosch/Mercedes system approved for Stuttgart Airport's P6 garage. That is robotics and vehicle automation, not a software-only AI agent.
Parking and retrieving cars means physically driving customers' vehicles, and an agent without a body cannot do this.
City codes such as Baltimore's require each valet attendant to hold a valid driver's license and be at least 18.

Bridgit's construction workforce-planning AI agents put together project teams, find available workers and suggest assignments, but planners review and approve the suggestions before any change is made.

Sir Robert McAlpine is rolling out AI workforce-planning software across its UK operations to replace spreadsheet processes. The software checks workers' availability, certifications, location and project experience, and forecasts labour needs.
Lumber's SmartPlanner automatically picks crews by availability, skills and proximity for construction scheduling and dispatch.
AI interviewer tools run parallel one-on-one stakeholder interviews and synthesize where stakeholders agree and disagree. This supports delegating question design, conversation and synthesis.

BA practice guidance in 2026 says AI can draft requirements, but a skilled analyst is still needed to tell whether the real problem matches what the stakeholder described. The human keeps final ownership of the requirements.
In the US, no licence is needed to work as a computer systems analyst, so no legal sign-off barrier applies.

Vendor and analyst comparison guides for software platforms are widely published online in 2026, so an agent that can browse can gather and synthesize this material end to end. These guides note vendor bias and the need to verify pricing and vendor viability, which supports keeping a human review step.

Structured product assessments profile enterprise vendors (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, ServiceNow and others) on features and roadmap. This is the kind of evidence an agent can collect and compare to draft a recommendation without a human doing each step.

Procurement guidance says to judge vendors on performance, governance, ROI and roadmap fit rather than feature checklists. That depends on internal requirements, budgets and existing systems, which usually sit with people and internal systems an agent may not reach. No licence or legal sign-off is typically required, but a human usually approves the purchase.

Vendors describe AI agents that run the maintenance paperwork from start to finish. They flag equipment anomalies, open CMMS work orders, order parts through the ERP, schedule technicians and draft service reports. These claims are self-reported, and no independently verified oilfield deployment was found.

Oil and gas work-order creation and maintenance scheduling are being automated. Manual creation reportedly takes 15–45 minutes per order, and the same pipeline is used in refinery and oilfield settings.

Under OSHA 1910.119(i), the employer must carry out a pre-startup safety review for new or modified facilities. A multi-disciplinary team of engineers, operations, maintenance and safety staff checks physically that installed equipment matches the design. This means humans have to be on site and accountable for installation and startup.

Electronic field-data and logbook tools such as MonitorPro MP-Field, SUEZ eRIS-LOG and Ambisis already handle digital entry, validation, audit trails and AI extraction of data from documents. An agent could do the record-keeping and file-maintenance steps end to end.

EPA Region 4 logbook procedure: entries must be contemporaneous, objective and legible. Hardcopy logbooks are bound and handwritten, and electronic entries need an audit trail. The observations come from the person in the field, so a human must supply or check the content.

Field logbooks are treated as accountable documents in enforcement proceedings, and the person responsible signs, dates and initials the entries. This comes from SOPs and QA plans, not from a licence requirement.

Computrition's AMPS add-on builds menus from a master menu, handling therapeutic diets and recipe substitutions. Vendors such as MealSuite and Menutech advertise automated or AI menu and nutrition planning for healthcare.

Nutrition and dietetics technicians plan menus with registered dietitian nutritionists for people with special nutritional needs. In clinical care they typically work under RDN supervision, so a human professional reviews the work.
A Brazilian school-menu tool generates weekly menus that meet nutritional references, but a nutritionist still chooses the final menu, so a human stays in the loop.

FDA-cleared home wearables such as Current Health and Mindray mWear automatically measure pulse, respiration and temperature and use software to flag changes. Software can then read, log and flag the data, but a person still has to put on, apply or operate the sensor at the patient's side.

In an Oxford hospital-at-home study, patients' own manual temperature readings were logged on only 51-58% of days, while the chest patch captured pulse and breathing rate much more consistently. Measurement still depends on someone being physically there.

Taking temperature, pulse and respiration is a standard aide skill, done non-invasively under RN supervision and reported to the supervisor. No licence requires a human to sign it, but it is a hands-on bedside task.

Vendors sell AI video analytics for casino surveillance. They say it flags dealer errors, odd hand movements, chip placement problems and suspicious betting, links play data with dealer rosters to spot collusion, and checks thousands of cameras automatically for scene compliance with regulations. These are vendor claims and have not been independently verified.

Nevada's surveillance standards set required camera coverage for games, the cage and count rooms. Only surveillance personnel and key employees may enter the surveillance room. The work is done through camera systems from a separate room rather than by handling things on the floor.

Surveillance agents must know the department's procedures, Gaming Commission regulations and minimum internal control standards. Under these rules, surveillance personnel are regulated staff with restricted access. The searches did not confirm the exact licensing requirements for these staff.

Michigan requires a case report for every body. It must list the personal effects that come with the decedent, the embalming details, and the name, license number and signature of each licensee who did the embalming. It must be kept at least 7 years.
Virginia requires a separate report for each embalming, with the embalmer's name, signature and license number, plus the supervisor's signature if an intern did the work.

Funeral home software already handles case management from first call to disposition, regulatory paperwork tracking and inventory. An agent could automate record entry and upkeep, but a person still has to look at and handle the clothing and valuables to list them.

Funeral home software such as MorTrack and Last Rites handles dispatch, vehicle tracking and allocating staff and vehicles. That covers only the planning paperwork around a procession, not the physical work.

State procession laws (Delaware, Kansas, New Hampshire) govern escort or lead vehicles driven by funeral home staff or police. Organizing a procession means a person on site driving and directing traffic.

The Tribute Technology 'Procession' product supports case and task management, so an agent could help with scheduling and notifying families. Placing the casket and leading the cortege still need a person there.

AI cameras at fixed sites can flag visitors who get too close to exhibits or cross set lines and alert a control room. Operators can then speak to visitors through two-way audio. This only covers fixed, camera-equipped venues, not moving tour groups, and the source is a vendor case study.
Tour guides are responsible for the group's safety and for keeping the group together. They watch visitors on the spot to make sure tour rules and safety practices are followed.

South Africa's Tourism Act requires registered tourist guides to take all reasonable steps to ensure the safety of the tourists they accompany. This puts a duty of care on a human guide in at least some jurisdictions. Australian training material says no licence applies to the guiding unit, so this varies by country.
HashMicro's AI agent records order requests, checks the details and creates sales orders with no manual admin work. It can also pull order data out of POs, PDFs and voice messages.
Jotform's AI Order Taker answers phone calls around the clock, collects order details and checks them in real time against existing form systems, so no staff member is needed.
Some AI ordering setups still have a human confirm orders or step in on complex or unclear cases. Accuracy depends on audio quality and how complex the menu or catalog is.

Employer and O*NET-style task descriptions say helpers thread conduit ends with a pipe threader, connect couplings and fittings with a wrench, and fabricate support brackets from strap iron with a hacksaw, shaping dies, hammer and punch, then bolt or screw the brackets in place. This is entirely physical manipulation on site.
In Maine, helper electricians are licensed and may make electrical installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician.
In Hawaii, unlicensed helpers may do electrical work only under a licensed journey worker or supervising electrician, who must be physically present at the project site.

The O*NET task list for Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00) describes this duty as physically raising, lowering or positioning equipment, tools and materials with a hoist, hand line or block and tackle. It sits alongside related physical duties such as rigging scaffolds, hoists and shoring.

OSHA requires a qualified rigger, meaning a person the employer judges qualified, when workers in the fall zone hook, unhook or guide a load (29 CFR 1926.1425(c)). It also requires one for hoisting during crane assembly and disassembly work (1926.1404(r)(1)).
Under OSHA, the employer decides whether a rigger is qualified, based on their knowledge, training and experience. For hoisting equipment rated at 2,000 lbs or less, a separate exception applies.

The MUTCD's automated flagger assistance devices (AFADs) still need a human flagger to run them remotely, either at one end of the work zone or from a central location. Flagging is not done autonomously by software.
Iowa's AFAD guidance requires trained flaggers on site who can switch to manual flagging if a device fails. Physical presence is needed.

State specifications require AFAD units to be linked and controlled by wireless communications with fail-safe behaviour. The devices are physical roadside hardware operated by people, not something a software agent would normally reach.

Clean-in-place (CIP) systems automate washing of pipes, vessels, tanks and fittings. They run on PLC/HMI controllers, not software AI agents, and people still have to clean the outside of equipment and the cooking area.

Automated CIP cycles push a pre-rinse, a caustic or acid wash and a post-rinse through equipment that is already in place. Hosing down, scrubbing and sanitizing the cooking area are still physical jobs done by hand.

CIP replaces a slow, hands-on routine of taking equipment apart and cleaning it by hand. That routine is physical work an agent with no body cannot do. At most it could start a CIP cycle that is already set up or log sanitation records.

Lifeguards already log weather, tides, water conditions, equipment checks and first-aid or rescue records on digital forms and apps such as SafetyCulture, SLSQ's LIMSOC and the SLSA Operations App. An agent could pre-fill the conditions data and turn a lifeguard's notes into structured reports.

Some regulators and governing bodies require signed and dated incident reports filed within set deadlines, for example Vermont's tramway incident form and New Hampshire's 5-day injury report. This makes a human who saw the event responsible for the content.

Alpine Canada's incident form must have all applicable sections completed and carries a signature and date block. Those details come from someone who was there and observed the injury and the treatment.
Robots that stir and pour pancake batter exist only as research prototypes that need robot hardware. A software-only AI agent cannot do this physical work.

Automated pancake makers are dedicated machines that dispense and cook batter, and the patent says pancake production is still mostly manual and labor-intensive. Physical handling is central to the task.
Commercial units like POPCAKE use pre-mixed batter bags in dedicated appliances. That is not something an AI agent working through software, documents or messages can do.

Commercial vivarium systems such as Setra and Rewire Neuroscience's Degrees of Freedom offer networked temperature and humidity monitoring with remote dashboards, mobile alerts and some control features. An agent with access could read data and possibly change setpoints, but these systems mostly monitor rather than adjust room conditions.

Remote control of vivarium devices through a web browser or phone app exists only in patents and research or hobbyist prototypes. Most caretakers in kennels, zoos, nurseries and farms adjust thermostats, heaters, humidifiers and vents by hand on site.

The Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and institutional policies require species-appropriate ranges, daily recorded checks and calibrated devices. They also note that conditions inside cages can differ from room readings, so on-site checking matters, but no law says a licensed human must make the adjustment.

A March 2026 paper describes agents that read files, run code, query databases and work across the research pipeline from literature review through analysis to drafting. They are strong on speed, coverage and method, but weaker on theoretical originality and tacit field knowledge, so a human still has to interpret and review.

Brookings says agents can now carry out social-science research steps on their own, but output quality can drop the longer an agent works on one task in a single session, so humans still need to review the work.
No US state licenses sociologists. The available certification (AACS) is voluntary, so the law does not require a human to do or sign this analysis.

Commercial AI tools (TherapyFuel in TherapyNotes, Twofold, Mentalyc) draft treatment-plan goals, measurable objectives and interventions from diagnoses and chart data. An independent review says clinicians still have to review and adjust the drafts for diagnostic nuance, risk and medical necessity.
In the MedicsCloud SUD EHR, AI generates ASAM assessments and builds problem lists that flow into treatment plans, so clinicians can move straight to goal setting.
Minnesota Stat. 245G.06 requires the individual treatment plan to be signed by the client and the alcohol and drug counselor, and to document the client's involvement in developing it.

Commercial AI chatbots and agents for higher education already handle program information for prospective students, application guidance, eligibility checks, course selection and enrollment changes. These are the main digital sub-steps of recruitment and registration.

Agent templates such as StackAI's Advising Assistant connect to student information systems to pull student records and match them against requirements. They support placement and registration advising, but a human advisor stays in the loop.

A 2026 academic comparison finds current advising chatbots mostly reactive. Students and advisors still have to build the academic plans themselves, so humans remain essential for personalized placement decisions.

A May 2026 study found that coding-assistant AI tools such as Claude Code could turn instructor-written course notes into lecture slides that were accurate, complete and pedagogically sound. A separate study found that students rated AI-generated slides about as highly as slides made by instructors.

At Acadia Divinity College, an AI avatar wrote the syllabus, scripted and gave lectures to graduate students, and graded their work. Students said they felt 'duped' and preferred a human professor, which suggests that live, trusted delivery still depends on a human.

The University of Newcastle used short lecture videos delivered by an AI avatar but kept in-person labs and live Q&A. Some students worried about losing engagement, so universities are adding avatars alongside human teaching rather than replacing it.

Agent layers that connect to Canvas through its APIs say they can write scores straight into the gradebook (LTI grade passback). Integration tools can push gradebook and completion data on to the SIS or a reporting system. This shows that entering, calculating and syncing records can be automated. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

In March 2026 Instructure released the IgniteAI Agent for Canvas, which runs educator workflows. It is still at the early-adopter stage, and its announced features do not mention gradebook or attendance tasks.

Under institutional policy, the instructor of record is responsible for making sure final grades are submitted for each enrolled student. Faculty must also follow FERPA when recording grades. So a human still has to review and certify the grade records.
Commercial AI chat agents run prospective-student engagement around the clock, answer program questions and sync leads to a CRM. These are the main digital recruitment sub-steps.
Agentic recruitment workflows can find students who left an application unfinished, send follow-ups on their own and pass cases to staff only when needed.

AI-agent advising chatbots help students build degree plans and give registration and placement guidance from catalogue rules. Faculty still handle in-person open houses, recruitment events and persuading students to choose a major or program.

NIH notice NOT-OD-25-132 says NIH will not treat applications substantially developed by AI as the applicant's original work. It also says NIH will use AI-detection tools and caps PIs at six applications per year. Because of this, the PI has to write and own the core of the proposal.
Limited AI help with grant applications is not banned. Applicants must check AI-assisted text themselves for plagiarism, made-up content and invented citations, so a human still has to review it.
NSF encourages applicants to disclose AI use rather than restricting it. This shows that AI drafting of proposals is already common and is accepted when the applicant is open about it.

A library has tried to automate end-to-end cataloguing with an AI system to reduce administrative load. Cataloguers still oversee the workflow, which means the cataloguing sub-step can be partly delegated but a human still reviews it.
Commercial AI agents already automate inventory tracking, reorder triggers and anomaly flagging. These are the digital parts of maintaining and distributing materials and equipment.

Scheduling agents organize staff schedules and track inventory, with a person reviewing the output. This covers the routine coordination sub-steps, but supervising workers in person in libraries and labs stays with a human.
Vital signs monitors can send readings straight into the EHR through HL7/FHIR middleware. This automates the recording step, but someone still has to physically take each measurement.

In a vendor-published case study, Welch Allyn monitors with Accelero Connect integration are used on a hospital's psychiatric unit. Staff say the main gain is no longer having to type readings in by hand.
Vendor material describes GE Carescape VitalsLink as sending readings wirelessly to the EHR, with nurses doing this at the bedside. The measuring itself is still done by a person with the patient.
Residence hall package software like Notifii Track lets staff log packages and automatically sends email and text alerts, with signature capture at pickup. A human still handles the items.
Parcel Tracker reviewers describe scanning a parcel and the resident being notified automatically. The scanning and delivery are done by hand by staff.

Student-housing mailroom software reads courier labels through a mobile camera to pull out recipient names and sends notifications across several channels. Only the data and notification sub-steps can be automated.

Palm Beach County bridges use edge video analytics that watch safety zones and automatically alert operators to breaches. At the Jupiter US 1 bridge, tenders watch AI thermal camera screens that pick out people, cyclists and cars before opening, and a LiDAR interlock blocks the opening if it senses motion. The human tender still makes the final check.

The Caltrans bridge operations manual says the drawbridge operator shall thoroughly check that all pedestrians and vehicles are safely behind the barriers and that the movable parts of the bridge are clear. This makes the human operator responsible for the check.
Some remotely operated drawbridges depend on a human remote operator watching CCTV and infrared sensors. Coast Guard rules for these bridges assume a human operator does this surveillance.

Vendors sell FP&A AI agents that track budget against actual spending on their own, look into variances and draft financial commentary. The figures they publish (for example, 60-70% less time spent) come from the vendors themselves and have not been independently checked.
Vendors also claim AI agents can analyse all budget-to-actual variances in real time, which suggests budget administration and report preparation can be handed off end to end.

Under 2 CFR 200.415, the fiscal reports and payment requests for a federal award must carry a certification signed by an official who can legally bind the recipient. That means a human has to approve and sign the expenditures and financial reports.

FDIC examination procedures include on-site checks such as surprise counts of vault cash and dual control over the vault and cash shipments. An agent with no body cannot do these physical inspections.

Vendors offer AI agents that check collateral eligibility, haircuts and concentration limits, and verify borrowing-base calculations with custodians. These are vendor claims, not independently verified deployments.

Reconciliation agents can investigate and propose fixes for securities and settlement breaks, but typical designs leave a human to approve the result. This fits a partial-delegation rating with human review.

Wardens collect wildlife data on the ground and from the air to estimate distribution and abundance, and they investigate water pollution and habitat damage. This fieldwork requires being physically present.
AI tools such as SpeciesNet can automatically detect and classify animals in camera-trap images. This speeds up the processing of survey data.
Camera-trap AI handles common species well but struggles with rare, small or similar-looking species and with changes in location. Workflows still rely on humans to validate the results.

The Salem, VA animal control SOP says the officer must unload every animal before doing paperwork. Each animal has to stay restrained by leash, snare pole, carrier or trap until it is placed in a cage or kennel run. Dangerous animals need a second officer present. The whole task is hands-on physical handling.
The Texas DSHS animal control officer training covers transport in cage-equipped trucks and careful handling to calm the animal. It describes this as manual work.
In the Salem SOP, the officer also has to clean and disinfect any body waste spilled in the unloading area. That step is physical too and no software agent can do it.

Inspecting a physical film print means winding the reels by hand on a rewind bench, feeling for splices and torn edges, looking closely with a loupe, checking reel flanges and remaking bad splices. All of this is hands-on work that an agent without a body cannot do.

For digital cinema packages (the digital equivalent of a print), software can check completeness and integrity automatically. ClairMeta and DCP-o-matic check file hashes, sizes, schemas and signatures, and can spot an incomplete transfer or corrupted files. Only this digital portion of the work could be handed off to an agent.
A DCP workflow guide says automated checks do not replace human playback review. Ingest and screening checks still take place on the cinema server inside the projection booth.

Replacing a projector sprocket is hands-on mechanical work. Taper pins are pressed in hard and take real effort to drive out, and the shaft must be supported so it does not bend or damage the sprocket. An agent with no body cannot do any of this.

The sprocket must fit the shaft with no play and without being too tight, or the picture will weave. Some swaps take about two minutes on the machine, but intermittent sprockets need precision tools and are often sent to a service station. The judgment and fitting are physical work.

Projection manuals describe spotting worn sprockets by checking the machine in person and seeing unsteady pictures or torn perforations. An AI could only help with the paperwork: looking up the manual, ordering parts, or writing a maintenance ticket.

O*NET says this occupation loads, operates, and sometimes adjusts and repairs mail processing, sorting and canceling machinery, and clears jams in sorting equipment. All of this is hands-on work on the equipment.
A private mail-sorting job posting describes sorter operators doing hourly hands-on barcode quality checks against a physical USPS template while running the machines.

The automated parts of the work, such as optical character reading and barcode sorting, are already done by the machines themselves. What the human operator adds is feeding mail, sweeping bins and clearing jams, all physical tasks a software-only agent cannot do. It could at most help with console or sort-plan software it would not normally have access to.

Commercial heat-detection systems (Heatime, ai24, SelectDetect, Afimilk) use neck-collar or pedometer activity sensors to flag estrus. An agent can read and interpret these dashboards, but only on farms that already have the sensors installed.

A neck-mounted accelerometer collar (RUMI) detected estrus with 90.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity in 47 Holstein cows and suggested insemination timing windows. This supports the monitoring/data side of the task, not physically handling the animals.

On pasture, neck collars work less well, so rump-mounted standing-behavior sensors such as Heat Switch were developed. Detection still depends on physical hardware on the animals, and exercising animals to induce estrus has to be done in person.

Machines fill, seal and print semen straws in one step at about 14,000 straws per hour. A person still has to set up and run them. Print data can be loaded from customer databases and linked to lab-management software such as Prism10 Bull. This means an agent could prepare the label data and keep the records, but the physical packaging cannot be done through software.
ICAR guidelines set the minimum straw identification: centre code, breed, bull ID and a collection code in yyddd date format. These are fixed data fields that software can generate.

CSS certification (a NAAB subsidiary monitored by USDA) sets standards for producing the semen and for what goes on the straw label. The search did not show any rule that a licensed person must personally label the straws.

VES DairyBOS is a cloud-based barn controller. It lets producers adjust ventilation, cooling and lighting and watch near real-time barn temperature and humidity from a phone or tablet. Software can therefore change setpoints when the barn is connected.

With AP Connect and Agri-Alert, swine producers can monitor and change temperature, humidity and static pressure settings from a smartphone. One producer changed a barn's temperature remotely after an alarm, so the adjustment step can be done digitally.

BarnTalk and Little Giant BARN-IQ sense conditions and send alerts when they go out of range, and BARN-IQ can switch smart-plug fans and heaters. Many barns still use local thermostats, heat lamps, curtains and inlets that a person has to set by hand, so physical presence and system access limit how much an agent can delegate.
Track brackets are fastened to jambs and headers with lag screws driven through brackets into the wood structure. The installer has to find the framing and drive the screws into it by hand on site.
The steps are hands-on: install wood bucks on masonry jambs, drill pilot holes and drive 3/8 in. lag screws with minimum edge distances. An agent can only help by looking up these specifications.
Fastening the track involves loosely attaching lag bolts, checking the track for level, then tightening them. Each step needs a person physically working on the track.

Load-planning software (e.g., SAP TM, ORTEC, Cargo-Planner) calculates load arrangement and sequence from freight dimensions, weights, and stop order. It applies LIFO, stackability, fragility, and axle-weight rules and produces 3D load plans, so the sequencing part of the task can be automated end to end.

Load-planning tools need structured inputs such as pallet and carton sizes, weights, and handling rules. A supervisor physically checking freight at the dock still supplies or verifies these inputs, including the condition, fragility, and actual dimensions of the freight.

Carrier and FMCSA guidance treats safe loading as something checked on site through physical inspection or supervised loading. No law or license requires a human to sign the sequencing decision itself.

Agency job descriptions say supervisors watch field work, train staff in MUTCD/ATSSA rules and inspect crews installing signs, signals, barricades and markings. This happens in person at the work site.

An AI assistant based on the MUTCD answers questions about where to place signs and flaggers and about temporary speed limits. It can help a supervisor with guidance, but it cannot direct crews on its own.

A research project (NCHRP IDEA 264) is building inspection software that uses vision-language models on dashcam video to check work-zone traffic control. It is still at the research stage, which points to partial help with inspection rather than full supervision.

Machines that paint nails automatically do exist, such as Clockwork's MiNiCURE. They use 3D cameras and AI to steer a robotic nozzle, so the job needs dedicated robotic hardware. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they cannot do this.
Clockwork's robot paints nails in about 10 minutes but is only in a few locations and does not cut or shape nails. Painting nails is a physical manipulation task.
Most US states require a cosmetology board license to do nails professionally. That means school hours plus written and practical exams, for example 300 hours in New Hampshire and South Carolina.

Stone chip repair is hands-on work: cleaning the surface, mixing and tinting polyester mastic with catalyst (100:2–3), applying it with a knife and polishing it. A digital-only agent can't do any of these steps.

A repair guide says to warm the stone with a small propane torch and work filler in while the surface is hot, then remove the excess with a razor blade. Handling the torch and judging the result by eye are both manual.

Chipped-marble repair means taping off the area, cleaning it with acetone and bonding with epoxy or marble cement. AI can only help with information such as product choice or color matching, which is a small share of the time.

Hobart's automatic wrapping system has a built-in scale and label applier; it weighs, wraps, computes the price and labels up to 30 packages per minute. It is a physical machine, not a software agent.
Mettler Toledo sells weigh-price labelers and the 880 Auto Wrapper for fresh meat in back rooms. The pricing and labelling are automated in hardware, but a person still handles the product.
Digi's AW-5600ATII and LI-700 II weigh, wrap and label meat automatically. The only parts software can reach are the label and price data settings.

Vendor 'Executive Recruiter Agent' products research senior candidates and deliver market analysis and curated shortlists, leaving relationship-building and negotiation to humans. This is a vendor claim, not independent evidence.
Executive search practice uses AI for sourcing speed but keeps selection and judgment human, and hiring outcomes depend on human oversight and governance.

Under Delaware DGCL §142, officers are chosen as the bylaws or the board determine. Appointment authority is a corporate act vested in accountable humans, not something that can be handed to an agent.

This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence. ChatFin says its FP&A agents watch general-ledger actuals against the budget and flag variances. It also says they trace each variance down to the transaction and write first-draft commentary and monthly business review decks.

This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence. The source says agents refresh rolling forecasts and automate much of the data gathering and analysis in FP&A. It does not say they replace human judgement on strategic development opportunities.

Another vendor, Tellius, sells agentic AI for finance that does automated root-cause and trend analysis on financial data. This supports L2-level delegation of the analysis sub-steps, though a human still prioritises the strategic opportunities.
Commercial AI tools such as Krea's Sketch to Concept Design turn rough sketches and text prompts into several clean, presentation-ready concept design variations.
Pencil is a commercial AI tool for 3D jewelry design, sold by subscription and used by brands for customer customization. AI can generate the design drawings for a craft object.

A 2025 study tested an AI image-generation tool for ceramic-craft design and found clearer design communication and better feedback. The students and instructors still made the design decisions, which suggests partial rather than full delegation.

Correction sergeant job specs say the role enforces rules on security, conduct, discipline and safety in person. That means supervising inmates at meals, recreation and in cells, searching for contraband and taking direct charge of disturbances, which needs a physical presence and command authority.

Policy-management platforms such as Lexipol supply legally vetted corrections policies and track acknowledgments, training and compliance reporting. This supports the 'maintain knowledge' part (looking up policies, summaries, updates), but I found no confirmed AI agent that enforces policy.
Sergeants investigate and report rule infractions to superior officers and may take command of the facility. These are sworn, accountable supervisory acts that a human must perform.

AI tools such as Taskade, Creately, Guidde and Process Street already produce housekeeping and room-cleaning SOPs, checklists and workflows, and can add approvals and task assignment. An agent can therefore draft the standards and procedures from start to finish.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 requires the employer to keep a written hazard communication program covering labels, SDSs, a chemical inventory and training. An agent can draft it, but the employer is responsible for it, and on-site checks of the chemical inventory are needed.

OSHA guidance tells employers to name a coordinator who assigns staff to tasks such as training. Putting procedures into practice means in-person training, inspection and enforcement with cleaning crews, which a human supervisor still has to do.

Velosi's housekeeping software covers supervisor inspection workflows, reporting of maintenance defects, and inventory of linen and amenities. These are digital supervisory sub-steps that software can run end to end.

OXmaint's AI takes work orders from the front desk, housekeeping, the guest app, IoT sensors and scheduled preventive maintenance, then classifies and prioritises them automatically. That covers the coordination side of supervising maintenance and repair.

AI scheduling tools assign and sequence staff using occupancy, check-out patterns and staff availability. The in-person parts of supervising laundry, valet and repair staff stay with the human: directing people on site, physical quality checks and handling problems. These figures come from vendor marketing and are not verified.
O*NET lists 'Move heavy furniture, equipment, or supplies, either manually or with hand trucks' as a core task for Janitors and Cleaners (37-2011.00). The work is all physical lifting and pushing.

Janitorial job postings include moving furniture and handling heavy loads. That takes a person on site, which a software-only AI agent without robotics can't provide. At most it could help plan the move or schedule it.
Janitors spend most of their time on their feet and sometimes lift or push heavy furniture or equipment. I found no licence or legal sign-off rule for this task.

To dust blinds you physically tilt the slats, vacuum them with a brush attachment from top to bottom, and wipe both sides with a microfiber cloth. That is hands-on work an agent with no body cannot do.
Hanging window coverings means measuring, marking bracket spots, drilling pilot holes and fastening hardware on site. All of it is physical manipulation.
Before taking draperies down you have to free hooks and rod hardware from the fabric, and you shake them out before washing. The only part software could help with is looking up care instructions.
Housekeeper job postings list moving and arranging furniture and turning or flipping mattresses as duties. These need someone physically present to lift and carry objects up to 40–50 lbs.
Postings require the worker to move dressers and flip mattresses without help, and to bend, squat, kneel and twist continuously. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
Some employers send furniture moves to maintenance staff, so this is purely physical labor. No licence or sign-off is involved.

Commercial software can turn flight data from an airport operational database (AODB) or other external systems into voice announcements. Vendors say it works with common PA systems such as Q-sys, Bosch and Honeywell, so routine arrival and departure announcements can run end to end without a person.

Text-to-speech is used for announcements at rail, metro and bus stations and at airport gates, and can be updated for schedule changes, delays and emergency alerts. Gate agents still make unscheduled live announcements that depend on what is happening at the gate, so a human stays involved there. The source is vendor marketing.

One search found no FAA or ADA rule saying a human must make PA boarding announcements. A DOT notice says carriers do not have to make a general preboarding announcement at the gate, and the Air Carrier Access Act deals with accessible information rather than who delivers it. The regulation text itself was not checked, so treat this as a likely finding.

Onboard harvester systems like Ponsse Opti and Log Max LogMate measure stems and optimize bucking in real time. They are machine control systems on physical harvesters, not software agents working without a body.

Waratah TimberRite handles real-time bucking optimization, stem measurement and production data logging on the harvesting machine itself. This shows that the measuring step depends on physical sensors at the log.

Skogforsk's 2025 wood value trial found that even automated harvester bucking loses value mainly through length and diameter measurement errors, so physical measurement at the stem is still the deciding step.

On harvester machines, the onboard computer decides where to cut using taper predictions and price lists ('bucking to value'). This runs as embedded machine control, not as a software agent, and an operator still has to be present.
Commercial bucking optimizers like Waratah TimberRite are onboard harvester control systems. They are tied to the physical machine.
In manual chainsaw bucking, the cutter makes the decisions out in the woods. The only digital help is simple tools like an Excel value matrix.

MSHA guidance says shot-firers carry radios close to electric blasting circuits. Each radio has a set minimum distance it must be kept from detonators. That makes setting up and placing the radio a physical, hazard-sensitive job at the blast site.

Wireless remote firing systems such as Austin Powder E*Star, Dyno Nobel SmartShot and Daveytronic send coded radio messages from a tablet or console. However, a certified blaster on site still runs them, and they rely on field hardware that an AI agent cannot reach.

MSHA blasting rules (30 CFR Part 75 Subpart E) put shot-firing and circuit-check duties on qualified people at the site. This leaves an AI agent only minor help, such as drafting message scripts or logs.

Parts are physically fitted and positioned by dedicated robotic hardware such as Voortman's fitting and welding machines, which align parts using hole-based positioning and laser scanning. A software-only AI agent cannot do this.

OSHA crane rules (29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC) require qualified riggers when workers hook, unhook or guide loads, and qualified signal persons when hoisting. A human must physically carry out the lift and take responsibility for it.
Signal persons must be qualified through a third-party or employer evaluator before they give any signals during crane operations.

Product is levelled on dryer belts by machines such as oscillating spouts and spreaders, set up mechanically for each product. This is equipment automation, not something a software agent does, and when it's done by hand it is physical raking or shovelling.
Inline dryer and roaster lines use mechanical spreaders (ramshorn, vibratory, oscillating belt or rake spreaders) to spread product on the band. All of these are physical machines.
Uneven bed depth across the belt leads to under- or over-dried product, so the task is physical handling of material on the line.

Press-brake control software can store tool and gauge-finger libraries and work out ram positions and backgauge settings automatically. That supports the planning side of setup, but a person still has to mount the dies and adjust the machine by hand.

When a die is replaced by hand, the operator works out the new die's interference region and limits the backgauge to stay clear of it. Patent US5211045 notes that a manual die change can lead to selecting the wrong die, so the work is hands-on at the machine.

OSHA 1910.217 covers die setters during die setting and requires the employer to train them and keep them competent. During die changes, lockout/tagout must be done by authorized employees in person. These are workplace-safety duties, not a licence or sign-off rule.

Furnace AI and advanced process control products, such as SMS group's EAFXpert and patented AI arc-furnace control, recommend or set power and electrode moves, and the patent also covers gas and oxygen supply. These are specialised control systems built into the plant, not general AI agents. Their public materials do not describe a general agent controlling burners or fuel on its own.

A patent describes AI that could recommend or apply moves such as electrode position, voltage and current, natural gas and oxygen supply, while avoiding hazards like water ingress. This shows the setpoints can be reached through software, but only via the plant's own control systems.

NFPA 86 says people who run furnaces must be trained by a qualified person, show they understand the equipment, and take regular refreshers covering startup, shutdown and lockout. Safe furnace work assumes trained staff are on site, checking the equipment hands-on.
Wire brushing is a hands-on surface-prep step done before plating. The worker has to remove rust, dirt and grease from the actual workpiece, because any spot left uncleaned will not plate.
Wire brush cleaning means physically scrubbing the material's surface, and the brush hardness and pressure have to be controlled by hand. A software agent with no body cannot do this.

Community-built MCP servers (adobe-mcp-indesign, lucdesign/indesign-mcp-server, NilasA indesign-mcp) let AI agents control InDesign directly: placing text, applying styles, laying out pages and exporting. Several describe themselves as experimental or proof-of-concept, and their stated tool counts are inconsistent.
Vendors connect AI workflows to InDesign Server to build complex documents and layouts automatically, which supports headless, template-driven page make-up. This is the vendor's own marketing claim.

Practitioners mainly use AI to write InDesign scripts. Forum experts report that AI-written scripts are often broken and that AI cannot yet do real page layout on its own (a 2025 opinion), so a human still needs to review typographic and layout quality.

O*NET lists this as a task for Stationary Engineers and Boiler Operators: helping plumbers repair or replace water, sewer or waste lines, and with daily maintenance. It is hands-on physical support work.
The occupation's repair duties include overhauls and replacing defective valves, gaskets or bearings. These are physical jobs on equipment and piping.
Other job-profile sources describe helping plumbers with line repairs as an occasional, on-site helper role.

Belt-scale integrators such as Thermo Scientific Ramsey work out belt loading, flow rate and total tonnage automatically. They can be monitored from a networked PC or a web interface, and some, like Belt-Way Plant Connect, report through cloud or mobile apps. So the 'read conveyor scales' part can be done in software if the scale is networked. Putting materials on scales or measuring them by hand still needs a person on site.

NIST Handbook 44 Section 2.21 requires every belt-conveyor scale to have a built-in audio or visual alarm when flow reaches 100% or more of rated capacity, or falls to 20% or less. The overload check is therefore already done by the equipment, so the human or agent only monitors it and responds.

Scales used for buying and selling (legal for trade) need NTEP certification and sealing by weights-and-measures officials. That rule covers the device, not the person reading it. No licence is needed for an operator to read a scale.
Tools like CraneTime already handle tower crane scheduling digitally, aiming to remove booking conflicts and keep teams coordinated, so this mostly digital task can be automated in part.
Delivery scheduling software for construction, such as Canary Wharf's Zone Manager, matches deliveries to crane and hoist slots. That covers the 'determine sequence of deliveries' step of the task.

HeviLift, used by PCL, simulates thousands of possible lift sequences and their cost and schedule effects. The operator still has to turn special loading instructions into how the crane is actually run on site.

Tool crib software (ToolWatch, CribMaster, ShareMyToolbox) only logs who checked a tool out and when it is due back, using barcode, RFID or badge scans. A person still has to carry the tools physically, so software only handles the small record-keeping part of the task.

Bluetooth tags can find tools and send an alert when a tool leaves the crib. That helps someone locate a tool but does nothing to move it, which needs a body or a robot. The reference agent has neither.
Most steam-table tools only log hot-holding temperatures and water levels; staff still enter the checks by hand. I found no software agent that refills food or equipment.
Steam-table automation hardware such as Eagle AutoFill senses and refills water in the wells, not food. Physical restocking of pans, utensils and bar supplies stays manual.
Restaurant sensors can flag when storage inventory is running low. This helps with deciding when to restock but does not do the physical replenishment.

Landscape software such as Aspire already handles crew scheduling, route optimization, sending work orders to crew phones and geofenced time tracking. These are the digital sub-steps an agent could run.
Foreman job postings describe on-site work: setting the day's work list, working alongside crews pruning shrubs, coaching pruning technique and inspecting finished work in person.
Foremen must make sure crews follow safety procedures, wear protective equipment and use machinery safely, which takes in-person supervision.

Landscaping equipment apps such as SafetyCulture link each machine to its maintenance and usage history through QR codes or asset tags. Crews scan the codes on site to run inspections and report problems. That means a person has to handle and look at the equipment, while the software holds the records.

Asset Panda's guidance for landscaping inventory uses barcodes as unique IDs, pulls up each item's lifecycle details when scanned, and can import existing spreadsheet records. This is the digital record-keeping and reconciliation work that an agent could take over.

A trade article on keeping maintenance trailers organized says supervisors must check tools and materials in person ('inspect what you expect'). Counting stock and judging whether items still work requires being there physically.

Landscape field-service platforms such as Jobber, Aspire and RootControl already record crew hours by GPS and produce timesheets, proof-of-work records and automated reports. General tools like ClickUp Brain flag missing entries and summarize tracked time, so most of the compiling and formatting can be automated.

Pesticide application records are required, but any format is accepted as long as it contains the required data, such as product, site and date. The rules require keeping the records, not that a human writes them. The facts recorded still come from what the crew did in the field, so a supervisor must supply or check them.

Under EPA rules for commercial applicators, records must be kept and made available for inspection for at least 2 years. The applicator or supervisor stays responsible for their accuracy, so a human review step remains.

Field-service time tools such as QuickBooks Time and Hubstaff record crew clock-ins with GPS and geofences, send clock-in reminders and send time cards to managers to approve before payroll. An agent could compile timesheets, reconcile them and flag errors, but a manager still approves them.

ClickUp's AI marketing page for landscapers says its assistant can chase missing time logs, flag overtime and summarize labor hours. Workstatus says it tracks time-off requests. This is vendor marketing, not independent proof, but it suggests the processing sub-steps can run on their own.

Under the FMLA, the employer must send eligibility and designation notices within 5 business days and handle medical certifications. Management makes the decision, and mistakes create legal risk, so leave approvals need a human judgment and review. No law says a human must personally sign them.

Commercial platforms such as GreenSight TurfCloud and AerialData Turf Health Explorer use drone multispectral and thermal imagery with NDVI analytics to map turf stress. That lets software help with remote condition assessment, but a person still has to fly the drones or capture the imagery on site.

AerialData drone surveys find turf stress that cannot be seen from the ground and show it as hotspot maps. The analysis is useful, but the walk-through inspection of plants and soil (touch, soil probing, pests, close looks) is still done in person.

Dronifi and Pix4D/TerraView tools use computer vision to flag encroachment, irrigation problems and moisture issues from aerial data. An AI agent could interpret these outputs, but it cannot physically tour the grounds.
Vendors sell email triage agents that classify incoming mail by intent, urgency and topic, then send it to the right department or person for reply.

A 2026 vendor blog describes AI triage that classifies, routes and prioritizes inbound email, with routing rules and escalation of unclear threads to a human. Figures such as about 70% of mail auto-routed are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

In shared inboxes such as Front, AI triage runs on top of a rules engine that routes by sender, keyword or tag. Routing is a software step: no physical presence and no licensed sign-off is needed for digital correspondence. Paper mail would first have to be scanned.

Online certified-mail services let a user upload a document, enter addresses, choose USPS Certified Mail and an electronic return receipt, then review and pay. The provider prints, assembles and mails the item, so records that are already digital can be sent without anyone handling them.

Commercial platforms such as Quadient ConnectSuite e-Certify and SimpleCertifiedMail through Endicia automate certified-mail preparation, tracking and electronic return receipts, and say they connect to existing systems or APIs.

When the records are paper files, someone still has to gather, copy and put them in envelopes, attach PS Form 3800 and the green card, and drop them off for mailing. An agent without a body cannot do these steps, so a human is still needed for that part.
Vendor-reported: AI agents for manufacturing planning feed demand forecasts into MRP and calculate material needs such as safety stock and consolidated purchase orders inside ERP systems.
Vendor-reported: QAD describes agents that check inventory and capacity across ERP systems and propose schedule and material changes for a human to approve.

Vendor-reported: SAP cloud ERP offers real-time MRP, demand-driven replenishment and AI-agent production order release. The task is calculation on software and data the clerk already uses, and no licence or physical step is needed.

Sage Intacct's 2026 R2 release includes AI-driven line-level matching of purchase orders, receivers and vendor invoices. It flags differences in quantity and price automatically and uses tolerance thresholds, so the document-to-document comparison step can be automated.

Vendors such as Veryfi offer AI that extracts and matches data from bills of lading, purchase orders and invoices, which reduces manual intervention. These sources are vendor marketing and do not include independent accuracy data.

O*NET 43-5111.00 describes the work as largely clerical but tied to physical goods. Workers weigh, measure and check materials, and they remove loads that fail standards. Reading the actual labels, tags and tickets on shipments requires someone on site or scanning equipment there.

This task is manual earthwork done on site with picks, shovels, pneumatic tampers and rakes. A software-only agent with no body or robotics cannot dig, backfill or compact soil. At most it could look up grade specs or compaction guidance, which saves very little of the working time.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(k), a competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems every day. The inspections happen before work starts, as needed during the shift and after every rainstorm. The competent person must have authority to correct hazards on site.
OSHA's interpretation letter says 1926.651(k) is cited when no competent person is available to do the daily inspections. That means a human with on-site authority is required by law.

AI and telematics tools can monitor engine hours, oil pressure, and hydraulic fluid temperatures to schedule or predict maintenance. They only flag the work. Humans still do the greasing, cleaning, and repairs.
Equipment must be de-energized and locked out before anyone cleans, maintains, or repairs it (29 CFR 1926.417), and the work itself is done by hand with hand and power tools on site.
Job postings for repair and maintenance laborers list hands-on preventive maintenance, hand and power tool use, welding and grinding, and following lockout/tagout procedures.

O*NET lists 'Provide assistance to craft workers, such as carpenters, plasterers, or masons' as a Construction Laborers task (importance 68). The neighbouring tasks are hands-on: erecting scaffolding and tending pumps for concrete and plaster.

Helper duties include supplying materials to masons, mixing mortar, plaster and grout by hand or machine, holding tools and materials, and cleaning work areas. All of this requires being on site and handling things physically.

A state job classification describes the work as helping carpenters erect scaffolding and helping drywall plasterers apply finishes. This is physical labor on construction sites, which a software-only agent cannot do.

To secure a mirror, a worker screws a J-channel into the wall studs, applies beads of mastic to the back of the glass, sets the heavy glass in place and clips it while the adhesive cures. All of this is hands-on work that an agent with no physical body cannot do.

The guidance on which mastic to use, where to support the mirror and how long it cures is already in manufacturer documents, so software can only help with looking up information. It cannot do the act of securing the mirror.

Mounting guides describe hand steps: leveling the clips or channels, placing the adhesive and getting the screws into studs. None of them mention a licence or sign-off needed to install a mirror. This was checked against DIY and trade guides only, not legal sources.

Faux finishing is hands-on work done at the wall. The painter puts on a base coat, then dabs glaze with a sea sponge, bunched rag, stippling brush or comb, and has to work wet glaze across a whole wall in one session. An agent with no body can't do any of these steps.

Rag rolling means applying glaze with a roller and lifting it off with a rag by hand. Software can only help at the edges, for example by looking up glaze ratios or mocking up colors. It can't do the core work.
Guides recommend testing the technique on scrap board or a hidden area first and choosing the base coat sheen on site. These are physical judgment steps that need someone present.
Pipe-zone backfill goes in lifts of 8 inches or less, and each lift is compacted by hand tamping or mechanical means without damaging the pipe. This is physical work done in the trench.
Bedding and backfill must meet required compaction levels (for example 6-inch bedding at 90% relative compaction), which crews achieve on site with equipment.
Heavy compaction or vibratory equipment has to be kept about 0.9 to 1.2 m from the pipe, so the work relies on hands-on handling of equipment and material in the field.

O*NET lists 'Dig out sewer lines manually, using shovels' as a Core task (importance 63) for Septic Tank Servicers and Sewer Pipe Cleaners (47-4071.00). The task is manual excavation, so it needs a person on site using hand tools.
The occupation is about cleaning and repairing septic tanks, sewer lines and drains in person, including fixing breaks in underground piping. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

O*NET lists this task for occupation 49-2011.00. It involves taking machines apart by hand and inspecting wires, gears and bearings with hand or power tools and measuring devices, which is physical manipulation.

A posting for an ATM cassette repair technician describes the job as hands-on: troubleshooting with hand tools, replacing worn parts, cleaning mechanisms and calibrating to the manufacturer's specifications.
O*NET says the occupation includes travel to customer sites for service or emergency repairs, so the technician has to be there in person.

Fleet maintenance software (Fullbay) builds repair estimates from labor time guides, parts data, PM history and live parts pricing and availability, so most of the estimating work is already automated.
ShopView's heavy-duty truck labor guide advertises VIN-specific labor times and AI-generated estimates and work orders from a repair prompt. These are vendor claims, not independent tests.

ARI offers AI labor guides that find parts and labor line items and move them into quotes or invoices, which covers the main pricing sub-steps. A technician still has to diagnose the fault and confirm the scope before the estimate is used.

Line installers dig the ground open for underground cable with trenchers, cable plows, borers and digger derricks, and then lay cable in the trench or in conduit. This is physical, on-site work with heavy equipment.

State dig laws (for example Washington RCW 19.122 and Colorado) require a locate request through 811 two to three business days before digging. An agent could file this request online, but it is only a small part of the task's time.
Under Idaho law the person who actually does the digging is responsible for making sure the locate request was made and pays for any damage. That puts the liability on the human excavator on site.
O*NET lists the task as attaching, altering and trimming wire, insulation and coils with hand tools. This is hands-on work at the bench.

Related tasks are also physical: cutting, stripping and bending wire leads with pliers and wire scrapers, and lining slots with sheet insulation. Software agents without robotics cannot do any of this.
This is a production job and needs no licence. The only barrier is physical manipulation, and the reference AI agents have no body.

Vendor says its bakery vision systems could signal oven controls to change zone temperatures, belt speed or steam injection when bake color drifts, in near real time. The wording is conditional and comes from the vendor.
Camera inspection links pale or dark crust to oven temperature drift, conveyor speed changes and steam-injection timing errors.

Vision platforms can send rejects and alarms through PLC/MES, the plant-control link that automatic adjustment depends on. Without camera feeds and networked oven controls, observing and adjusting stays physical and on-site.

Research in 2025-2026 shows LLMs can edit and optimize existing CAM-generated G-code. In one small test on a single Haas machine, ChatGPT-revised code cut cycle time by about 37%. Commercial CAM agents, such as Cimatron's shown at IMTS 2026, generate toolpaths automatically. So the editing step itself can largely be done in software.

LLM G-code generation still needs syntax and geometry checks plus correction from user feedback (GLLM self-corrective approach). A human or simulator therefore has to check the code before it runs on the machine.

Operators usually change programs in Edit mode on the machine's own control panel and save them there. They also adjust feed overrides and tool offsets, and confirm changes with test cuts. Spotting problems like chatter, tool wear or out-of-tolerance parts, and checking the fix, takes physical presence at a control that is often not networked.

Vendor tools such as Workerbase's Troubleshooting Agent pull machine error history, SOPs and OEM manuals together to suggest fixes for alarms at the machine. The operator still asks the questions and does the work, so this helps the human rather than replacing them.

Shop-floor monitoring agents can spot anomalies and send information to the right person. That covers the routing and drafting parts of escalating a problem, but someone at the machine still has to observe and report the fault.
