Customer contract clauses hold further fabrication until the first article is accepted. The approval comes from authorized people in the quality system, not from the operator, and no law requires a human operator to perform this step.
O*NET lists cleaning machines, tooling or parts with solvents or solutions and rags as a task for CNC tool operators. This is hands-on physical work.
In shop practice, operators sweep, mop and use degreaser and shop rags on the machine, the work area and the inspection table. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

The other option is automated parts washers, which are physical equipment, not AI agents. Manual solvent cleaning also requires PPE and disposing of used rags as hazardous waste. This source is a vendor selling parts washers.

Mills automate board measurement and cut marking with dedicated scanners and optimizers built into the production line. These are physical sensors and machinery, not software agents. An agent with no body cannot handle a ruler, square or caliper on a workpiece.

Optimization software and the cut markers or projectors it drives (for example VAB's Pointer Projector) need scanning and marking hardware installed in the mill. An AI agent could at most do the small calculation part, such as cut lists and tolerance checks.
Vision systems that check cuts and grades are scanning hardware fixed on the production line, which shows that checking cut accuracy depends on physical sensing rather than on digital documents.

Automatic lubrication pumps (e.g., Graco G3) can be programmed to deliver lubricant to bandsaw guides and bearings, but these are physical machine systems that humans still have to install, refill and clean. They are not AI agents. A sawmill has 300-500 lubrication points.
In sawmills, lubrication programs mean hands-on work at each lubrication point. Software can only help with scheduling and tracking.
In a hardwood mill, the shift from manual to automatic lubrication was a hardware change. It still needed physical maintenance and a choice of lubricant.

Vendors say agentic systems already watch chemical-plant process data and flag anomalies before normal alarms go off, and claim deployments at over 30 plants. These are press-release claims, not independent results. Celanese's JO.AI reportedly uses an anomaly-flagging agent across 50 plants (secondary source citing Forbes). Yokogawa says its FKDPP AI controlled a chemical plant on its own for 35 days.

In PSM-covered processes, operator rounds still include physical field checks: local pressure and temperature gauges, tell-tale gauges, tank levels, heat tracing and taking samples. An agent with no body cannot do these.

Vendors sell wireless instrumentation to digitize manual gauge rounds because charting gauges by hand is time-consuming and error-prone. This suggests the digital share of monitoring is growing but many plants still do it manually. OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119) requires trained operators and management procedures, but I found no rule that only a human may read instruments.

PLC-controlled CIP systems already automate the rinse, chemical and final-rinse phases. They switch between acid, alkali and hot-water phases and control flow and temperature, but this is dedicated plant automation that has to be pre-installed. A software agent cannot do this on its own.
Mobile CIP units run on a Siemens S7-1200 PLC with pneumatic valves. Someone still has to bring the unit to the equipment and connect it physically, which needs on-site manual work.
Plants without CIP clean tanks manually, and operators handle hoses, valves and chemicals by hand. Automating this needs a physical retrofit that an agent with no body cannot carry out.

O*NET lists this as a core task for SOC 51-9012.00, with an importance rating of 82. It covers installing, maintaining or repairing hoses, pumps, filters and screens on processing equipment by hand with hand tools, so it needs a person physically present.

In this occupation, workers set up and tend filter presses, shaker screens, centrifuges and stills on the shop floor. A related task is clearing clogs from machines and screens, which is also physical work done on the equipment.

An AI agent without a body or robotics cannot use hand tools. Its only possible help is minor: looking up part specifications or repair manuals, or logging maintenance work orders. That is a small share of the time spent on the task, which is why share_delegable is 5.

Electronic batch record and MES products already log material moves, parameter readings and equipment data automatically. They time-stamp each entry against the master record and flag out-of-tolerance values for review by exception. This means an agent connected to these systems could fill in most of the forms.

Vendors say batch records combine automatic equipment and automation data with operator entries. Manual inputs are still needed for observations that are not instrumented, and a person has to physically read those at the mixer.

21 CFR 211.188(b)(11) requires batch records in regulated industries to name the person who performed, supervised or checked each significant step. If equipment did the step automatically, the record must name the person who checked it. So a human still has to sign or verify.

One vendor describes an AI loop where sensor signals such as vibration, temperature and cycle data feed an anomaly detector, which sends early-warning alerts to maintenance staff. On instrumented equipment, software can do the detect-and-notify step. This is a vendor workflow template, not an independent study.

Predictive-maintenance products and research systems use machine-learning anomaly detection on machine data to flag malfunctions and cut unplanned downtime. They only work where machines are fitted with sensors and connected to software. The figure of up to 50% less downtime is a vendor citing a McKinsey survey, and I could not confirm it.

Retrieval-augmented generation (AI that looks up stored records before answering) can pull up equipment performance data when an anomaly is detected, which helps diagnose the problem and notify operators. Intel presents this as an illustrative design, not a deployed product. A production helper's task is mostly watching machines in person on the plant floor (sight, sound, smell), and an agent with no body and no connection to plant sensors or cameras cannot do that.

O*NET lists 'Remove products, machine attachments, or waste material from machines' as a core task (importance 69) for Helpers--Production Workers. It sits alongside other hands-on duties such as loading and unloading machines and moving materials.

Helpers support production workers by doing less-skilled manual work on the plant floor. Removing parts, attachments and scrap means physically handling them at the machine, which a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do.

O*NET lists 'Wash work areas, machines, equipment, vehicles, or products' as a supplemental task for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00). The occupation is described as lower-skill help duties, including cleaning work areas and equipment. All of this is hands-on physical work.

Related O*NET tasks for this occupation, such as cleaning and lubricating equipment and doing minor machine repairs, also need someone physically present to handle tools and machines. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of it.

Under 49 CFR 240, anyone who moves a locomotive, including a remote control operator (RCO), must be a certified human engineer. Certification covers skills tests, rules tests and vision and hearing standards. Remote-control operation still needs a person on site using a belt-pack controller, and a 2026 bill would ban remote control locomotives on main lines.
The FRA final rule of April 2024 requires a minimum of two crew members on board most trains. Moving to one-person crews or to full automation would need special approval or an exemption.
Remote control locomotives move trains in yards only through a human RCO who is physically there. Driverless trains are purpose-built, railroad-specific control systems, not general software agents.

Railroads such as Watco and Conrail put rulebooks, timetables, bulletins and special instructions on crew iPads through Comply365, with automatic updates, alerts and compliance tracking. Software can therefore check that the digital copies are current, but someone still has to check the paper binders and the device in the cab.

Under FRA rules, Form F6180-49A must be displayed under a transparent cover in a conspicuous place in each locomotive cab, and inspection records must be kept in the cab. These are paper items on the locomotive, so someone has to be there to confirm they are present.

ÖBB's infraDOAS tablet app downloads timetable data, orders and speed restrictions to the driver's cab, checks that they are valid and displays them. This automates the 'is the documentation current and available' part when the documents are digital.

Biomni is an agent built on large language models that writes and runs code. It completes biomedical research sub-steps such as causal gene prioritization, rare disease diagnosis and protocol generation without task-specific setup. These results are reported in the authors' preprint and have not been independently validated.

The ToolUniverse cancer-variant-interpretation skill takes a gene, variant and cancer type. It runs an 8-step workflow over CIViC, OncoKB, cBioPortal and ClinicalTrials.gov and outputs a report that tiers the variant's clinical actionability (T1 to T4). It was last updated in August 2026.

VariantBench tests agents on 118 variant discovery and interpretation tasks taken from published studies. The best reported pass rate was 42.1%, so expert review is still needed. Studying mutations also involves wet-lab work such as sequencing, cell and animal models, and mutagenesis, which agents cannot do.

Chainsaw maintenance is hands-on work: taking off the bar and chain, soaking and scrubbing them in degreaser, clearing the bar groove and oil holes, and filing the cutters with a round file or power sharpener.
Sharpening means filing each cutting tooth at its own alternating angle and filing the depth gauges every few sharpenings. A person has to handle the tool to do this.

Lubrication and pre-use checks (bar and chain oil, greasing the nose sprocket, chain tension, the chain brake, the air filter) are all physical inspection and adjustment on the jobsite. Software can only offer checklists or reminders.
O*NET lists this as a core task for Tree Trimmers and Pruners. It sits next to running chipping and shredding equipment and feeding limbs and brush into the machines.

A municipal job specification describes raking or shoveling debris into piles, loading it onto trucks or into a chipper, and hauling it away. Every one of these steps is manual or involves driving a vehicle.

Tree-service job postings for this duty require lifting up to 50 lb and working outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent can at most help look up a disposal site or plan a route, which is a tiny share of the work.

Under OSHA, line-clearance tree trimming means pruning or clearing trees within 10 feet of energized power lines. It is regulated hands-on field work that only qualified line-clearance tree trimmers may do, and it requires the worker to be physically present.

29 CFR 1910.269 applies to line-clearance tree trimming done by qualified employees. Unqualified workers have to stay at least 10 feet away from overhead lines, so the work legally needs trained and qualified people.
Workers have died during tree trimming near power lines. That is why OSHA stresses qualification and on-site safe work practices for this kind of manual work.

The task means putting a thin coat of sealant by hand (brush, tub or aerosol) on the exposed wood right after a cut is made on a live tree. That is physical manipulation an agent with no body or robotics cannot do.
Modern guidance mostly advises against routine wound dressing. The only digital part (looking up whether to seal, for example for oak wilt in season) is a small advisory share of the task's time.
Arborist sources describe sealant as a practice used at the site of the cut, with no licence or sign-off needed to apply it.

AI video tools such as HeyGen can produce retail tutorial and demo videos with avatars and voiceovers. That means an agent can write the instructional content, but the worker still delivers the live, in-person instruction.
Tools like TutorialAI generate step-by-step product guides and demo videos automatically. This covers preparing instructions for altering a product, not hands-on teaching on the shop floor.

Vendors describe AI demos that walk users through workflows and adapt to them. These work for software products; altering a physical product means a person has to handle and show the item, and the search found no evidence of in-store AI assistants doing this.

A model voucher works like an invoice. It records the client, job details, dates, working hours and the pay rate, and both the client and the model sign it when the job ends. Filling in the fields is clerical work an agent can draft from booking data, but the hours actually worked and the client's signature come from the set.

Agency terms set the billing rules, such as a half day being 4 hours, overtime rounded up to the next full hour, and fittings paid at 50% of the hourly rate. An agent with software access could apply these rules to calculate the amounts.
Model booking apps let clients book and schedule models through the platform, so booking data such as rates and booked hours is digital and an agent could reach it.

Generic AI booking agents already capture and qualify leads, book appointments on a calendar, send reminders and re-engage past clients. That covers the scheduling and outreach steps of arranging parties.

AI receptionists for event businesses answer calls, book consultations and trigger follow-up sequences from CRM data. This is the closest match to booking parties, but no party-plan-specific agent for recruiting hosts turned up.

AI tools for direct sales cover lead generation, outreach drafting and follow-up. Recruiting hosts, though, relies on the seller's personal network and persuading people face to face, and the parties are usually held in person. I found no licensing rule that requires a human to do the work.

FedEx's Pickup Request API lets software check pickup availability, schedule a courier pickup and cancel it. A successful booking returns a confirmation number, so the core booking step can be done end to end with no human.

Microsoft Dynamics 365 Intelligent Order Management lets users assign FedEx and UPS carrier pickup schedules to a fulfillment source. Its carrier API then sends the next available pickup time, so arranging pickups is already built into commercial software.

Logistics vendors sell AI agents that compare carrier rates, apply routing rules and confirm bookings on their own. This is the vendor's own marketing claim, not independent evidence that the agents work.

Loading a copier means doing things by hand: pull out the tray, adjust the length and width guides, fan and square the paper stack, place it within the fill line and reinsert the tray. A software-only agent cannot do any of these steps. Its only digital part is confirming the paper size and type on the control panel.
Manufacturers' manuals describe hands-on steps: setting the guides to the size marks in the tray and loading paper with the correct face up or down. A person has to be at the machine to do this.

Guidance for shared office copiers is about physically putting white paper in Tray 1 and colored paper in Tray 2, then picking the tray on the touch screen. AI could only help with the small digital step of selecting the tray or setting.

Optical sorters with cameras and AI already grade produce such as potatoes by size, shape, color and defects. These are dedicated machines with ejectors, not software agents, and the claims come from industry sources.
Vendor AI sorting systems, such as Robovision's, classify items from images and still need physical hardware with conveyors and ejectors to sort them. Feel and smell are not captured digitally.

USDA grading is voluntary for most produce. Licensed graders are needed only for official grades, for example under marketing orders, for import or export, or for government purchases. Ordinary sorting on a packing line needs no licence.

John Deere Expert Alerts and Remote Diagnostics analyze telematics data. With the owner's consent, they flag likely component failures to dealers and let dealers read or reset trouble codes and update software remotely. That covers the digital side of spotting faults and sending notifications, but not the physical repair.

The AI tools built for farm machinery, such as Deere Operations Center PRO Service and AGCO Fuse, mostly read fault codes and suggest likely causes through chatbots. Hands-on checks like listening for abnormal sounds, feeling vibrations, tracing hydraulic leaks and replacing parts still have to be done in person. This source is an opinion-style analysis, not vendor documentation.

Vendor 'AI diagnostic agents' announced in 2026, such as THINKCAR Tyler, help with diagnostic workflows and repair planning for road vehicles, not farm machinery. A technician still does the physical repair. These claims come from a press release and have not been independently checked.

Crew-management apps already let managers assign jobs with a field location and instructions, record hours, and tag harvest entries to the crew that picked them. That digital scheduling and tracking is the part an agent could take over.
In AgCrew, foremen and field leaders still assign the tasks and send the daily summaries. The software supports a supervisor who is in the field and does not replace them.
FieldClock schedules and projects labor for seasonal harvest and H-2A crews. That covers the planning sub-steps, but directing and watching workers in the field still needs a person there.

Semi-automatic transplanters need people to separate seedlings and feed them into the planter by hand. Fully automatic transplanters are mechanical equipment, not software agents, and they still need humans to restock plants.
Automating seedling pickup and feeding depends on physical robotic mechanisms, and most fully automatic transplanters are still at the prototype stage.
Robotic transplanting machines were built to automate feeding and inserting seedlings, work that used to be done by hand. This shows the task is physical manipulation.

Feed suppliers already run online ordering portals. MyForFarmers lets farmers place compound and blend feed orders at any time from a phone or computer and track delivery status, so an agent with computer use could do the ordering and delivery steps.
FeedX tracks tons of feed on the farm, projects the next delivery date from usage and lets users choose delivery dates. Scheduling and reordering are already automated in software.

MetaFarms Feed Mobile has staff place feed orders that a back office then reviews and approves. Human approval of orders is still common, and on-farm stock levels often still need someone to look at the bins.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.266(e)(2)(x) says the chain-saw operator must clear brush and other obstacles from the cut and retreat path before felling. The worker has to do this by hand on site with a chainsaw or axe, so a software-only agent cannot do it.
Kentucky's FACE hazard alert for loggers recommends clearing escape paths after the fall direction is set and before the tree is felled. This is a physical job done at the stump.
NCDOT's safety procedure for tree felling and chainsaw use under 1910.266 treats clearing and felling as hands-on chainsaw work. Software or AI agents have no part in carrying it out.
Logs have long been marked by striking an owner's mark into the log end or side with a stamp hammer. A lumberjack swung the hammer against the log to mark the trees they had cut.
Modern log identification uses paint, forestry hammers and tags applied by hand to the wood. The marks show origin, species, an inventory ID number and the licensee.
State harvest-marking procedure lists physical tools (marking guns, marking paint, a Biltmore stick) and requires marks that logging contractors and equipment operators in the field can understand.

Under 49 CFR 213.233, track must be inspected on a set schedule by a person the owner has designated under §213.7. The inspection is visual, on foot or from a vehicle, and devices may only supplement it. The qualified inspector must start remedial action immediately when a defect is found.

Automated track inspection systems use sensors and AI mounted on rail cars and do detect geometry defects. In December 2025 the FRA approved a 5-year waiver that lets railroads reduce visual inspections where these systems are used, but it does not remove human visual inspection.
Automated track inspection depends on hardware mounted on rail vehicles, so a software-only agent cannot do it. Without a waiver it cannot replace required visual patrols.
Railroads paint stencils such as 'UPRR Main Trk' and 'No Trespassing' straight onto the rail web or onto signs at the track. This is hands-on work done in the field with paint and stencils.
Vendors sell ready-made rail stencils and regulation decals. An agent could at most order supplies or look up the required text, which is a small part of the task.
FRA rules (49 CFR Part 215 Subpart D) cover stenciling on equipment, but no licence requires a specific human to paint signs. The deciding barrier is that the work is physical.

O*NET lists 'Set up and adjust equipment used to excavate geological materials' as a task for Helpers--Extraction Workers. The same listing includes hands-on duties such as loading materials and repairing drilling equipment with hand tools, so the work is done in person on site.

Rig automation exists, but it is built into the machines rather than run by a general AI agent. Epiroc RCS 5 lets users make or edit drill plans remotely, and Cat MineStar automates drill cycles and tramming. Physically positioning, rigging and adjusting equipment still needs people at the site.
MSHA 30 CFR Part 48 sets training requirements for mine workers. These cover who may work on site but do not require a licence holder to sign off on equipment setup.
Mounting an outboard is hands-on work. The technician sets the cavitation plate level with or just below the hull bottom and tightens the mounting bolts to spec with a torque wrench.

The sea trial checklist has the technician run the motor at trolling speed and full throttle, check the cooling water telltale, and inspect for fuel, water, exhaust and oil leaks. All of this needs someone on board operating the boat.
Under state law, a person operating a motorboat must hold a boater education card and carry it on board. California, for example, requires a California Boater Card for all ages since 2025.

Engine stand manuals say the engine is lifted with a crane or hoist, bolted through the stand's fingers at the mounting holes, then slowly lowered so the stand carries its weight. The mechanic has to do this with their hands.
Small engines are often taken out of the equipment frame so the mechanic can reach the parts. This is physical disassembly that software cannot do.
Lifting points, mounting bolts and torque values come from the engine service manual. Looking these up is the only part an AI could help with, and it is minor.

Curved pressing forms such as tailor's hams are used to shape sleeves, darts, collars and curved seams. The worker positions and moves the garment over the form by hand while applying heat and steam, so the task is entirely physical.
In pressing over a curved form, the garment is placed and held on the form and pressed with a hot iron and steam. A software-only agent with no body or robotics can't do any of these steps.

A standard ham can't handle every curve, so custom forms are made for different shapes. Each garment needs hands-on judgment about which form to use and how to manipulate it, which an AI agent can't do.

Blocking means stretching the garment by hand on a board to the exact size it should keep, then applying steam with an iron and a damp cloth and leaving it in place until dry. All of this is physical handling of the fabric, so a software-only agent can't do it. At most it could look up target measurements, which is a tiny part of the time.

Steam blocking needs judgment by hand: the worker controls how close the steam gets so stitches don't flatten or go shiny, and pins and shapes the garment from the shoulders down. No digital tool handles this.
O*NET lists pressing machine operator as a title for this occupation. The work means putting garments on heated presses and running them by hand, which is physical machine-tending.
Small garment presses, such as VEIT's collar and cuff press, are steam or electric machines that a person loads and runs by hand. No software agent can run them.
Making a necktie includes handling the fabric by hand, such as pinching the V-tip, which needs physical dexterity.

One 2024 study used the Prophet time-series model on existing operating data to spot early impeller wear in pumps used for fabric dyeing. That is software helping with diagnosis. A person still has to do the repair.

Vendors sell AI predictive-maintenance and maintenance-management software for jet, jigger, winch and beam dyeing machines. It predicts pump and bearing failures and creates work orders. Technicians still do the cleaning, oiling and part replacement by hand. These are vendor marketing claims that no one has checked independently.

A Birlasoft case study reports that machine-learning predictive maintenance at a textile mill cut asset downtime by 48%. It used more than 2,000 sensor points and was not specific to dyeing machines. The software helps plan the work, but the maintenance itself is physical and done by people on the floor.

Industrial automatic winders handle unwinding from spools and rewinding onto take-up packages with mechanical tensioners, joiners and conveyors. This automation is mechanical hardware, not a software AI agent, and any manual work left over is hands-on handling of spools, bobbins and yarn ends.

Rewinding means pulling yarn off a bobbin, running it through a tension device and slub catcher, and winding it onto a tube driven by a traverse drum. Every step is physical manipulation of material, so a software-only agent with no body cannot do any substantial part of it.
A traversing winding device can rewind spindles on demand along a textile machine. This shows the task gets automated through machinery, not through digital tools an agent can reach.

Research systems use cameras and AI on extrusion lines to flag surface defects in real time, so shop-floor workers can respond quickly. Detecting the defect can be automated, but people still act on the alert.

A vendor proof of concept for extrusion quality control shows defect alerts to operators on screen and can feed real-time feedback to the line. It is not a verified production deployment, and directing workers to adjust the machines stays on the plant floor.

Vendor material says AI vision raises an alert on the first out-of-spec section, which supports automated notification. This is vendor marketing and unverified. It is not evidence that a software agent can direct physical machine adjustments.

Distressing is done by hand: hammers, chains or nails dent the surface, screwdrivers or chisels cut gouges, a wire brush scrubs out soft fibres, and sandpaper rounds edges, all before the stain goes on. An agent with no body can do none of this.

The antique look also comes from hand work during staining: stain is wiped off with a rag so it stays mostly in recesses, and wear marks are placed where use would naturally leave them. This needs hands and eyes on the actual piece.

The worker uses judgement on the actual object, for example not sanding through thin veneer on particle board. Software can only offer general advice, so it cannot meaningfully speed up the physical work. No licence or legal sign-off applies to this task.

Tire building means physically placing the inner liner, plies and other rubber parts on a building drum, either by hand or with machine appliers on the factory floor. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent cannot do.
The O*NET profile for Tire Builders describes building rubber treads and layers onto tire casings in production and retread shops, which is manual or machine-operated physical work.
A process study of tire building notes that most steel-belted radial tires are assembled by hand: the inner liner and plies first, then the belts and tread.

Emerson's Winblend software runs batch blending by weight. Before a batch starts, it checks that raw materials, routes, flow paths and tank storage are available, and it logs alarms and completion data. This means the control and recordkeeping steps are already handled by software, not by an AI agent.

ABB's Regulatory Blend Control starts and stops blends, controls pump sequencing and adjusts flows to match a recipe. These functions run inside the plant's own control system, which an outside agent would not normally be able to reach.

In a 2008 case study, a PLC touchscreen panel let operators pick a recipe and dosed preset quantities. Lining up valves and hoses, connecting tanks and taking samples on site are still physical jobs for the operator, so an AI agent could mainly help with recipe calculations, checks and logs.
Continuity tools like SyncOnSet and DH Hair | Makeup handle continuity photos, notes and looks digitally. Someone still has to take the photos and enter the information on set.

Commercial tools such as Perfect Corp's AI Makeup Transfer can read color and texture from a reference look and suggest brand-specific product SKUs. These are guesses, not a record of the products the artist actually used.
Australia's CUAMUP412 continuity unit treats record-keeping and continuity photos as an on-set job, checking the performer's makeup at the end of each take. That requires being physically present.

No AI tool turned up that inspects installed wallcovering seams. The closest machine-vision work checks the alignment of finished tile installations from images and is meant to replace subjective visual checks. That means a human would have to take photos on site before an AI could even assist.
Commercial AI vision tools check pattern alignment and defects only in textile manufacturing, not on wallpaper already hung in a building.
Pattern-alignment algorithms for repeating patterns exist, but they plan cuts for garment seams. They do not inspect finished installations.
TSA's CT checkpoint scanners can detect explosives and other threat items automatically, but a TSA officer still looks at and resolves any bag the system flags.

A DHS S&T-funded AI algorithm piloted at Las Vegas flagged CT scans that might hold threats. It served as a second set of eyes for the officer doing the manual review and still needs TSA certification before deployment.

Regulators require people who operate X-ray or EDS equipment to hold certification and pass standardized image-interpretation tests. For example, CASRA reports that EU Regulation 185/2010 requires this.
RTSM/IRT platforms like ClinPhone Pro track site stock and automate restocking, which covers the digital inventory side of supply management but not physical storage.

Viedoc's trial supply management sends alerts when stock at a trial site falls below set threshold levels. An agent could use this for inventory planning, but a person still has to shelve, label and set up the equipment.
Signant's GxP Inventory is a 21 CFR Part 11-compliant software tool for tracking inventory. Arranging the physical space still depends on hands-on work at the site.

Accenture (Dec 2025, vendor forecast) describes PE teams moving from AI-assisted analysis to agent workflows that scan markets, test scenarios and flag diligence issues, with diligence becoming a continuously updated model.

DiligenceSquared, a Y Combinator startup, uses AI and voice agents to produce M&A commercial diligence research and claims, without independent verification, quality comparable to consultancies at much lower cost.

Epiq sells an AI assistant for HSR premerger compliance that tags and queries deal documents. Epiq says it can cut data-related filing costs by up to 80%, but the HSR filing itself still goes through counsel and the parties.

Optilogic, a vendor, says its AI-native supply chain design platform has autonomous agents that build network models, generate scenarios and weigh tradeoffs. This covers the analytical design steps of the task.
A 2026 trends piece expects companies to let agents recommend critical supply chain decisions but not commit to them. Humans still approve and carry out redesigns.

A Databricks-hosted vendor paper cites a Gartner prediction that 50% of supply chain management software will include agentic AI by 2030. This suggests agentic supply chain tools are still being adopted rather than fully autonomous.

Budgeting tools for wind O&M already exist: K2 Management and Emerson's P50 Booster, built on multi-brand SCADA data, forecasts maintenance needs to show owners when to budget for maintenance and to address rising opex.
In the vendor guide, agents run the annual planning process while finance keeps decision authority and the budget still goes to the board for approval. A human remains the final reviewer.

As of August 2026, FP&A agents from Cube, Datarails, Vena, Anaplan, Pigment and Workday work on top of existing Excel or planning models, but some deeper planning agents were still in beta. This is a vendor-written ranking, not an independent benchmark.

In 2026, AI permitting tools mostly check applications before filing. For example, Yuma AZ's January 2026 pilot reviews plans and documents for missing information and inconsistencies before submission. Vendor tools such as PermitOS and Datagrid claim to pre-screen applications against regulations and to connect to permit portals. Fully automated approval has only been announced, by Dubai in August 2026 for villa permits.

Dubai Municipality is building an AI agent to issue villa building permits without human review, which shows agencies are moving toward digital end-to-end processing. That example covers villa building permits only, not demolition or remediation permits.

Demolition permit applications usually need an owner or applicant signature, sometimes notarized. They also need an asbestos survey done beforehand by a certified inspector or licensed contractor, and some jurisdictions require a licensed PE or architect certification. So a human has to sign the application and provide licensed inputs, even though an agent can compile and file it.

AI-generated or AI-assisted sustainability claims on websites, packaging and ads can draw regulator scrutiny if they are inaccurate, vague or unsubstantiated, and agentic AI with little human review is flagged as a concern. This points to a human review step before publication.

The EU EmpCo Directive (2024/825) applies from 27 September 2026. Under it, general claims such as 'green' or 'sustainable' must be proven by the business. The Green Claims Directive's mandatory prior verification of claims is still a stalled proposal. Liability falls on the company, and no rule requires a licensed human to author or sign the material.
Implicit environmental claims made through imagery, branding and design must also comply, so a human still has to check generated visuals and wording against evidence and brand approval.

Standard and harmonized fuel cell test protocols and design-of-experiments methods are published and can be used to plan tests. An agent can draft test matrices, factorial designs and procedures from them.
Commercial ML tools such as Monolith already predict test outcomes and recommend which fuel cell tests to run next. This speeds up the planning sub-steps.

Running a test program means designing and building physical test rigs, often automated in LabVIEW. It also involves handling hydrogen safely on site and using station hardware, which needs people in the lab.
Applying a chemical that alters living tissue counts as the practice of medicine. Doing a chemical peel needs a physician, or a licensed practitioner the physician has delegated to.
State rules limit chemical peels to physicians, PAs and CNPs, and some procedures need a prescription from a licensed clinician.
AI tools for chemical peels only analyse skin and help with planning, for example measuring pigmentation and texture before a peel. A clinician still makes the call and does the procedure.

Digital pathology platforms such as Proscia Concentriq AP-Dx (new 510(k) in August 2026) and PathAI AISight Dx (July 2025) are FDA-cleared for primary diagnosis from whole-slide images. They are image management systems, so a pathologist still reads the slides and makes the call. The search turned up no autonomous AI diagnosis product.

PathAI's AISight Dx digital pathology system received FDA clearance for primary diagnosis in clinical settings, so slide images and lab data can be reached through software where labs have gone digital.

Under CLIA (42 CFR 493.1273(d), as quoted in CMS survey reports, not checked against the regulation text), a tissue pathology report must be signed by a qualified person. An electronic signature has to be authorized by the person who did the examination and made the diagnosis.

Commercial drug-diversion and supply-surveillance products (Bluesight ControlCheck, Wolters Kluwer Sentri7, Iatric DetectRx, Imprivata) pull data from dispensing cabinets, EHRs and timekeeping systems. They reconcile dispense, administration, waste and return records, and use machine learning to flag problems. Most still send the flags to a human to review, so an agent could handle the data-monitoring part but not the whole task.
Cloud software from Kit Check and Omnicell tracks controlled substances and combines charting and dispensing records so deviations show up as they happen.

DEA rules (21 CFR 1304.11) require a physical inventory of controlled substances at each registered location, with exact counts for Schedule II drugs. That is hands-on counting and record-keeping by the registrant, so someone has to be physically present and a licensed person is accountable for it.

Pipelines already pull EHR data automatically into REDCap-based registries for rare diseases. A multi-institution rare-tumor registry imported 482,450 lab results for 1,109 patients with high accuracy.
Vendors sell LLM and agentic workflows that find registry cases and extract data from clinical notes. They still put a human abstractor or reviewer in charge of the final decision.

Under HIPAA, patient data can be shared for research only through a signed patient authorization, an IRB or Privacy Board waiver, de-identification, or a limited data set with a data use agreement. These steps need human consent, oversight and accountability.

Endoscopy technicians physically handle biopsy forceps, polyp snares, clips and retrieval nets, and collect and label specimens, all under a physician's direct supervision. This is bedside manual work that a software agent with no body cannot do.
The role is performed under the supervision of a registered nurse and physician, and snare positioning and polyp removal are framed as actions taken under physician direction within clinical scope.

The existing AI in endoscopy is FDA-cleared polyp-detection software (GI Genius). It overlays alerts for the clinician and does not do the technician's hands-on assisting, and the clinician makes the final decision.

Appriss Retail runs a generative AI tool on Azure OpenAI that automatically links theft, fraud and abuse incidents into cases by matching suspects, narratives and vehicles. Its case-management module captures incidents and evidence, and manages suspects and resolution.
My LP Portal offers an AI loss prevention assistant along with incident reporting and investigation management, aimed at small retailers that have no LP department.

LP incident reports bring together a timeline, the people involved, and evidence from CCTV, POS records, alarms and witness notes, written in neutral factual language. Because such reports may be used in later legal proceedings, the investigator who saw the events needs to confirm and attest to the account.

Camera health monitoring software already checks each camera, NVR and network link on a set schedule. It reports tampering, blurring, blocked views and equipment failures in near real time, so an agent could handle the CCTV status-check part of this task through software.

Remote monitoring for sensor-tag (EAS) systems shows up mostly in patents, not in shipping products. The patents describe extra hardware such as acoustic or optical sensors to detect alarms, and they note that store staff have little control over these systems. Checking that EAS gates and locks actually work still usually means someone walking tags through the gates and trying the locks on site.

NFPA 72 requires alarm inspection and testing to be done by qualified, trained or certified people, and many states also license the companies that do it. This applies to fire alarms that contractors service. It does not require a loss prevention specialist to sign off on routine checks of security systems.

Sandwich and salad assembly is being automated only with dedicated physical robots (Nala Sandwich Bot and Bowl Bot, Bizerba's two-arm station at EuroShop 2026), which are outside the software-only reference technology. Even Sweetgreen's robotic line still has staff handle the start and end of the process and add final toppings.

Salad robots like Sweetgreen's Infinite Kitchen and Chowbotics' Sally work by physically dispensing ingredients, which shows the task is physical manipulation that a software agent with no body cannot do.

The FDA Food Code requires a Certified Food Protection Manager on site. Food-handler cards for line staff are a state-by-state choice. These are food-safety rules, not a requirement that a licensed human perform or sign off on each item.

Third-party guides say HubSpot's Breeze agents take one campaign goal, plan a multi-channel campaign, and draft and schedule content. They also warn that drafts often need editing to match brand voice, so a human still reviews the work.
A med-spa vendor (unverified claim) says AI agents can run live Meta and Google ad campaigns through official ad-platform connectors, but says the campaigns still need daily management.
In 2026, spa and salon AI tools are mostly sold for booking, reminders, loyalty and follow-ups; much spa marketing is still done by hand.

Commercial wetstock monitoring systems such as TankStream read tank contents and sensor packs every 20 seconds and upload the data automatically. An agent could watch that data, flag problems and keep the logs.
Biofuels take up water, which makes sensor-based water detection unreliable. Degradation can also speed up later in storage, so physical sampling and lab tests are still needed.
Good practice calls for physically sampling the tank bottom at several access points, draining free water and checking visually for haze, darkening or particulates. All of these need someone on site.

Housekeeping for combustible dust is physical work. Plants clean by vacuuming, sweeping or water wash-down, and they clean and inspect priority areas daily. Compressed air is allowed only after ignition sources are shut down. An agent without a body cannot do this cleaning; at most it can help draft the written housekeeping schedule.

Federal OSHA has no standalone combustible dust standard. It enforces housekeeping through the General Duty Clause, 1910.22 and a National Emphasis Program that covers wood dust. These rules require a clean workplace, not a licensed human to do or sign the cleaning.
Guidance for 2026 on combustible dust points to NFPA standards and dust hazard analysis. The cleaning itself is still done by hand with approved vacuums and similar equipment.

Commercial and public AI grant tools such as Polco's Grant Writing AI Agent and Massachusetts' GrantWell already match municipalities to funding, summarize funding notices, draft narratives and letters of support, and help with budgets. That covers most of the writing and research steps.

For local-government recycling grants such as EPA SWIFR, the governing body typically passes a resolution naming an official to sign the application and later grant documents. So a human authorized representative has to approve, certify and sign.

State recycling grant signature pages require an authorized representative to certify that the governing body approved the project. Applications also depend on internal program data, budgets, matching-fund commitments and partner letters, which a person has to gather and review.

Geothermal loop fields use HDPE pipe made to ASTM standards. Installers join it by hand on site, using socket fusion for smaller pipe and butt fusion for larger pipe. That means cutting, facing, heating and joining with fusion equipment.

PE industry guidance says operators who do butt fusion or electrofusion should be trained, pass an exam and hold an approved-operator badge, renewed every one to two years, following ISO/TR 19480. National schemes include Germany's DVGW GW 330.

ISO/TR 19480 sets out how PE fusion operators are trained, assessed and approved, which makes fusion jointing a qualified human trade. Software can only help with side work such as looking up fusion parameters or reviewing joint logs.

Agentic AI in regulatory affairs can run a linked chain of detecting regulatory changes, analysing them, drafting, sending notifications and keeping audit trails. It can also check internal policies against new or updated regulations. Qualified regulatory affairs, quality assurance and qualified person (QP) staff remain responsible for decisions.

Generative AI speeds up drafting of GxP standard operating procedures (SOPs), but it may not know the company's own processes and can produce outdated or wrong text. The sponsor stays fully accountable for any content the AI drafts.

Under 21 CFR 820, executive management is responsible for the quality policy and must set up quality system procedures. A designated person has to review, approve, sign and date the documents. Implementing a procedure also involves management approval and training.

Before a transfusion, two people (a transfusionist and a witness) must check the blood product against the patient at the bedside. Administering blood requires an authorized licensed provider such as an RN, LPN or physician.

Bedside barcode systems such as BloodTrack Tx (FDA 510(k)-cleared) electronically match the patient to the blood unit and record vitals and reactions. These are documentation and checking aids, not autonomous administration.

Current reaction detection uses rule-based alerts on vital signs that nurses enter, which can start a reaction work-up. The search found no autonomous AI tool that detects or manages transfusion reactions.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.703 says forms must be built, supported, braced and maintained to carry all expected vertical and lateral loads. Erected shoring must be inspected before, during and after the pour, and sills and base plates must be in firm contact with the ground and the form. All of this is physical work and inspection done on site.

Formwork automation is still physical robotics and only semi-automated, for example the DokaXbot Lift and the DoKart 3 table-form mover. That is outside what a software-only AI agent can do. At most, an agent could help look up specs or bracing layouts, which takes up very little of the task's time.
In precast plants, formwork robots run from CAD data place parts automatically. These are physical machines, not software agents.

Bosch's ESI[tronic] diagnostic platform is getting a conversational AI assistant, set for global rollout with the 2026/4 release. It checks vehicle diagnostic data against OEM repair guidance, schematics and Bosch's repair database. So an AI can interpret scan data and choose tests, but a technician still connects the tool to the car and takes physical measurements.

The TEXA IDC6 AI Diagnostic Assistant uses a control-unit scan and VIN confirmation to pick the vehicle, then guides the technician through each stage of diagnosis and suggests repairs. The software does the analysis, while hands-on testing stays with the human.

Most US states have no general mechanic license, and ASE certification is voluntary. Licenses are required only for specific jobs such as state safety or emissions inspections and handling refrigerant under EPA Section 609. So no law requires a human to perform or sign routine electronic component testing.

Installation manuals show the job is mostly hands-on work: mounting and leveling the unit, attaching duct collars and insulated ductwork, running sloped condensate drains with traps, and connecting electrical power. An agent can only help by looking up specifications and sizing.

Under EPA Section 608 (40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F), anyone who services equipment that could release refrigerant, or adds or removes refrigerant, must hold technician certification. Uncertified apprentices must work under close supervision.

Commercial dehumidifier manuals require specific electrical connections, drain piping and service clearances to be done on site by qualified installers. No current software product does any of this physical work.

An October 2026 demo at the Bharat Diamond Bourse (BOTS.Ai) showed AI agents that price stones from the 4Cs using live market and recent-sales data. Rapaport is testing agentic AI for diamond market analysis and trading search. Both suggest an agent could handle research, pricing and online matching of buyers and sellers, though neither is shown to be in full production use.

Buying secondhand precious metals and jewelry falls under state rules: sellers must show government ID, dealers keep records and must hold items for set periods. These are compliance steps, not a requirement that a licensed human sign. Florida even allows ID checks through a national verification provider.
Maine requires dealers to check a government-issued ID and hold acquired precious metals for a set time. Handling the goods, inspecting them and keeping custody still need a person on site.

The AI cabin-inspection tools that exist need a person or a robot on board to capture images. Diehl's ACIRTo classifies defects from photos that crew take. DrumView, a research project running until the end of 2026, uses a mobile robot to find surface defects. A software-only agent would still need someone physically present to inspect or photograph the cabin.

DrumView is still a research project. It uses a robot that moves through the cabin and cameras with anomaly detection to find scratches, seam deviations and discolorations. Fully automated inspection is not yet a mature, available product.

A flight attendant union document describes 14 CFR 121.309 as requiring a preflight inspection. Crew must confirm that the required emergency equipment is on board and readily available, and must report anything missing or inoperative to the Captain. Under this reading, crewmembers do the check in person and are accountable for it.

Dispatch platforms for chauffeur, limo and private-hire fleets already sell AI auto-dispatch, smart driver assignment and 24/7 AI voice booking agents. That covers much of the request routing and information exchange between dispatch and drivers.
Industry writing on AI dispatching says routine trip assignment and status updates can be automated, but exceptions and situations happening on the road still need human judgment.

FMCSA rules ban drivers of commercial vehicles from using handheld phones while driving and allow only hands-free use. This is a safety rule on how the driver uses the device. It does not require a human to do the communicating, which supports automated, hands-free status messaging.

Machines that clean aircraft exteriors are physical robots that a person operates on site (for example, Nordic Dino's semi-automatic robots). They hold only about 5% of the exterior cleaning market. A software-only AI agent can't do this kind of hands-on work.
The vendor says its robotic washers can cut exterior cleaning of a wide-body aircraft from about 6 hours to 2. Either way, the work takes physical equipment and someone on the ramp.

An EU-funded project (Aerowash II) developed an automated washing system with preset patterns for each aircraft model. That is robotics, not software an AI agent could run on its own. My search found no products for polishing specifically.

A 2026 preprint, Flowr, describes an agentic Procurement and Ordering Agent for supermarket chains. It writes structured purchase orders using replenishment signals, demand forecasts and supplier catalog data.
Vendors sell retail AI agents that watch stock levels, work out order quantities and send purchase orders to suppliers. These claims come from vendors and have not been checked independently.

Vendor material says retail inventory agents watch point-of-sale data in real time, spot demand spikes for individual products and decide whether to reorder. This covers the demand-based part of the task.
O*NET lists this as a desk clerk task. A DOL job filing describes it as physically moving pre-packaged breakfast items and coffee supplies to a self-serve area. Clerks don't cook.
Breakfast attendant postings describe the work as setting up and breaking down breakfast items and brewing fresh coffee. All of it is hands-on work that software can't do without a robot.
AI inventory tools such as WISK.ai can forecast food and beverage demand and suggest purchase orders. That covers only the small planning and restocking part of the job, not the setup.

AI and software tools exist for planning which gear a shoot needs. Studiovity turns script breakdowns into shot lists with lenses and camera setups for each shot. CineBag builds equipment lists that can be exported to rental houses. These cover only the selection and planning sub-step.

Camera operators rig and operate camera equipment and work with grip and electric crews to rig supports, dollies, track and lighting flags. They also lay out sets and furniture and handle heavy equipment. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Career descriptions say the job is physically demanding and involves assembling studio sets and arranging cameras and lighting on location or in the studio. No law or licence requires a human to perform or sign off this task.

Washing, peeling and cutting produce in commercial kitchens is automated, where it is automated at all, by physical machines such as the IMC MF5 peeler/washer and vegetable processors with cutting discs. These need a person to load and run them; software agents do not do this work.
Industrial automatic peelers, such as onion/garlic peelers rated at about 240 kg/h, are mechanical equipment that only does the physical handling of the food.

Even dedicated automatic peelers struggle with produce that is non-spherical or has tough skin. This shows the task is a matter of physical handling and dexterity, which a robot-free AI agent cannot provide.

Customizable bid sheet templates in PDF and image formats are widely available. They list the item description, starting bid, bid increment and bidders. An agent can fill them in and lay them out from an item list without help.
Mobile bidding and online form tools pick the winning bidder automatically and send bids straight into spreadsheets. This means much of the digital prep around bid sheets can be done in software.
The printed bid sheets still have to be placed next to each auction item. Stuffing envelopes and assembling gift bags are also hands-on work at the venue that an agent without a body cannot do.
Researchers scored ChatGPT against an ACSM-based rubric for 26 clinical populations. Its exercise recommendations covered only about 41% of the content expected in a gold-standard prescription.

A systematic review of generative AI for exercise prescription found that it complements expert guidance but does not replace it. In expert-rated studies, LLM programs were generally safe but not individualized enough to each person's health conditions and goals.

In Louisiana, clinical exercise physiologists hold a licence from the State Board of Medical Examiners and work under a licensed physician's direction, approval and supervision. Their licensed scope includes formulating and developing exercise protocols for cardiopulmonary rehabilitation.
CNA support work is hands-on: setting up suction equipment, giving oxygen with tents and masks, turning and positioning patients, and moving them with wheelchairs, walkers and lifts.
Current AI tools cover only the digital side, such as ambient sensing for fall risk and virtual nursing for documentation, monitoring and education. Clinicians still do the bedside care.
In 2026, nurse ambient AI produces flowsheet entries that a nurse must review, and only 22% of nurses surveyed said they trust AI tools for safe patient care.

Hospital food services use TUG robotic carts to move meal trays through hallways and elevators. Staff watch the carts on iPads and meet each one at drop-off, then take the trays to patients themselves. Robots are physical systems and fall outside the software-only reference technology.

Tray-delivery software uses barcodes on trays and patient wristbands, so staff can make sure the right diet goes to the right patient. Software can help with checking, but a person still physically hands over the tray.
At UCSF, the food-service TUG robots do not enter patient care areas. People still do the bedside serving and the collection of trays.

Heidelberg's Predictive and Remote Monitoring use sensors and algorithms to detect developing faults and flag them. The cause is then fixed by technicians or operators, so software handles detection but not the physical correction.

Prinect Inspection Control finds defects, sounds an alarm, inserts a tab in the pile and shows the defect on the console for the operator to correct. The response to the alert is left to the operator.

Press fault messages show where the fault is and guide the user through physically clearing jams or fixing components, and the manual warns against forcing paper out of the fuser or rollers. Resolving these faults requires hands-on work at the machine (evidence is from a Xerox digital production press, not an offset press).

Procurement sustainability agents, such as Dcycle's, rate suppliers using public ESG data (CDP, SBTi, controversy databases) and compare them against purchase history. This is a core sub-step of weighing environmental aspects of competing suppliers and merchandise.

myclimate Smart PCF uses AI to estimate the carbon footprint of individual retail products from attributes like category, price, weight and materials. This makes it possible to compare competing items automatically.

AI LCA tools for fashion and retail, such as Carbon Trail, fill data gaps with AI estimates, and no independent accuracy benchmarks turned up. A human still needs to check the outputs, get proprietary supplier data and make the final buying call. There is no licensing or physical requirement.

Heavy-duty diesel smoke testing uses the SAE J1667 snap-acceleration procedure. A light-extinction smokemeter is attached to a stationary vehicle that has reached normal operating temperature, at the roadside, a depot or a repair shop. Someone has to be there to fit the probe and work the throttle.

Under California's HD I/M program, newer vehicles can meet the requirement with OBD data sent through CARB-certified telematics, with pass criteria of no MIL-on events, no active codes and no permanent codes. That part could be automated in software. Non-OBD vehicles still need opacity tests at set intervals.

Tests submitted for compliance must be run by HD I/M Approved Testers using registered tools, or by certified remote OBD devices. This means a credentialed person or device is responsible for the result.

Canada's correctional service (CSC) is piloting an Accenture AI tool that reviews and organizes information from intake files to draft offender profiles. Staff still review the output, and critics point to the risk of automation bias.

South Korea's correctional service plans AI that combines counseling, disciplinary and medical records to flag signs of violence, self-harm and escape. The service says the AI's analysis will not decide treatment by itself, so humans keep the decision.
In job descriptions, supervisors read inmate records for health, safety and security concerns and recommend classification changes. This is document-based work in internal corrections systems.

Construction-intelligence platforms such as Buildots combine site data, BIM, schedules and daily reports to forecast delays and show their root causes at the activity level. AI can also link schedule updates, RFIs, change orders and weather records to support delay analysis. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.
AI agents can collect the reports, inspections, photos and training records tied to a safety incident and draft a root-cause analysis. Construction safety professionals still make the final call.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1926.20(b)(2) requires the employer to name competent persons to inspect job sites, materials and equipment frequently and regularly. A competent person must be able to identify hazards and have the authority to take prompt corrective action. Employers must also investigate recordable injuries and document them. This is based on secondary sources; the regulation text was not checked on OSHA.gov.

Agents can operate Revit through MCP connectors with over 226 Revit functions. Add-ins such as Glyph CoPilot and BIM Engine automate parts of construction documentation, like sheets, views, tags and dimensions. No independent benchmark shows agents reliably producing a complete permit-ready set without a human checking it.
Glyph CoPilot is sold as an AI assistant that automates construction documentation inside Revit.

In Washington State, a registered architect or engineer must sign and stamp each page of construction drawings submitted for a permit. They may seal only work they prepared or reviewed, and they carry full responsibility for it.

Vendor product pages say AI document tools pull fields from bills of lading, check that required fields and signatures are present, and match driver-uploaded BOLs and PODs to load records in a TMS. This covers the check of the documents themselves. These are vendor claims; no independent tests were found.

Freight-audit software from VektorTMS checks required BOL fields, verifies signatures and matches each BOL to its load, flagging missing data. This shows the completeness check can run end to end once the paper is digitized.

Under 49 CFR 177.817, a carrier may not accept or haul hazardous materials without a correct shipping paper, and the driver must keep it within reach in the cab. At pickup the driver still has to compare the paperwork with the actual freight (piece counts, seal numbers, placards) and sign the BOL, which needs a person on site and a responsible human.

In 2026, AI recruiting agents handle top-of-funnel hiring on their own: sourcing, screening, outreach, scheduling and first-round structured interviews, which end in a ranked shortlist for human review. Most deployments are only partly autonomous, and humans keep the later decision stages. These figures come from vendor sources.

The EU AI Act classes AI used for recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, promotion and termination as high-risk. That brings oversight, documentation and risk-management duties, so humans must stay responsible for personnel decisions.
NYC Local Law 144 bans automated employment decision tools unless they pass a bias audit each year and the results are published. This adds compliance limits on fully automated selection.

Mississippi board rules say anyone using an electric file in a manicure must first hold board-approved proficiency certification and display it to the public. A human must be licensed and certified to do this work.

South Dakota requires at least 8 hours of training, including hands-on practice and infection control, before anyone may operate an electric nail file or drill on clients. The task is physical, hands-on work.
Robotic nail machines such as Clockwork only paint nails. Reports say none of them shape or buff nails, and the task needs a body anyway, which software agents do not have.

Dealer management software (Autologica Sky DMS) already produces parts-order suggestions using 14 methods, including sales level, part value, aging and purchase frequency. This covers the digital side of maintaining stock without a person doing it by hand. Source is the vendor's own description.

A 2025 IEEE conference paper simulated AI demand forecasting with IoT/RFID tracking at a car dealership. Stock-outs fell from about 9.7% to 4.2% and inventory accuracy rose from 85% to 93.3%. These are simulated results, not a live deployment, and the setup still needs tagging and storage work on the warehouse floor.

A trades-business guide describes AI agents that log parts used, check stock levels and trigger reorders on their own. Physically finding parts on shelves, attaching labels and doing counts still needs a person, and an agent with no body cannot do those steps.

Private household cook duties include keeping records of menus, finances and other business matters. A typical posting asks the cook to log purchases, menu costs and kitchen expenses, stay within the household budget and report variances to the household manager.

Consumer AI apps such as Famally, EasyGrocery and Zenkitchen say they plan meals, build grocery lists, pull items and prices from receipt photos, and track pantry and budget. These are the main sub-steps of menu and expense record-keeping. The claims come from app listings and have not been independently verified.

Bookkeeping guides for personal chefs describe digital logging of grocery costs, fees and expenses. They also say household and business spending must be kept separate, which is a judgment call that may need a human check. No licence or sign-off is required for this kind of record-keeping.

Fitting brakes means removing the wheel and loosening and tightening pad bolts with an Allen key. The mechanic also has to line each pad up with the rim, set cable tension with barrel adjusters, then spin the wheel and test the brakes by hand. All of this needs hands on the bike, and an agent without a body cannot do it. At most it can look up specs or the right pad type, which is a very small share of the time.

Each brake has to be set to its own measured fit: the pad sits flush and square to the rim about 1-2 mm below its top edge, and the barrel adjuster is turned until the pads stop rubbing. These are hands-on adjustments, and no software or AI tool performs them.

Bicycle mechanics need no licence in the US or Canada. Certification, for example from UBI or Barnett, is voluntary, so there is no legal or liability rule requiring a human to do or sign off the work.

Software can work out spoke length from hub and rim measurements (flange diameter, flange-to-center distance, effective rim diameter, or ERD), but a person must take those measurements on the actual parts.
Online spoke calculators cover J-bend and straight-pull hubs but tell users to measure carefully and check the numbers before cutting spokes. Cutting and threading are done by hand with a machine.
Wheel builders say different calculators give slightly different results, so the final call on length and the hands-on build (lacing, tensioning, truing) stay with the human.

At Halton Healthcare, software creates the meal ticket from the patient's barcoded record and wristband (diet, allergies) and gives tray-assembly instructions. Staff still assemble the tray by hand and scan it before delivery.
Computrition's Tray InMotion software tracks trays from ticket creation, alerts staff to diet-order changes and checks wristbands. The physical work of putting food on trays stays with people.

On tray lines, printed menu tickets from the CBORD system list exactly which items go on each tray based on that day's menu and the patient's requirements. Workers then plate and assemble the trays by hand.

AI documentation tools such as AutoNotes and Mentalyc already draft SOAP, DAP and treatment-plan progress notes from session input or dictation, and AI note generation is described as reaching recreational therapy session documentation. The agent can write the note, but a human has to supply the in-person observations of how the participant is doing.

CMS therapy documentation rules for PT, OT and SLP require progress reports and treatment notes to carry the signature, professional identification and date of the qualified professional who provided the service. No CMS rule specific to recreation therapy turned up; the closest rules found were state ones (Texas, Arkansas).

State program rules (Texas YES Waiver) require recreational therapy progress notes with participant, date, times, service and location, written by licensed or certified providers such as a CTRS, so an accountable human has to review and sign.

Under 30 CFR 75.211, the roof, face and ribs must be visually examined, and sound or vibration tested where supports go in. Loose material is taken down by hand with a scaling bar from a safe position underground. All of this is physical work an agent with no body cannot do.
MSHA enforcement cases treat scaling as manual barring by a miner at the working face, using a scale bar or drill steel.

Under 21 CFR 211.84, workers must physically open, sample and reseal component containers so nothing gets contaminated, using sterile equipment and aseptic technique where needed. Samples taken from the top, middle and bottom of a container must be kept separate. All of this is hands-on work.

Each lot is held until the quality control unit has sampled, tested and released it, and sampling plans need a scientific justification that they are representative. That leaves accountability with a human or QC unit. An AI could still help work out statistical sample sizes and draft sampling plans or chain-of-custody paperwork.
Automated sampling systems in pharma are robotic hardware, such as isolators and aseptic bioreactor samplers, not software agents. A software-only agent with no body cannot physically draw samples.

NWCG S-130 Firefighter Training includes a required field exercise that can be arduous. The lead instructor must be a qualified Single Resource Boss and unit instructors must be qualified FFT1, so training is delivered in person by credentialed humans.
AI in wildland fire training appears as immersive simulation and visualisation tools such as UNSW iFire 1.0. These support human-led exercises; they are not autonomous instructors.
Commercial vendors offer virtual and simulator-based wildland fire training (FS3D/Intellic, DAS USFS simulator), but in-field hands-on instruction is still done by human instructors.

LLMs such as ChatGPT-4 produced understandable cataract-surgery education material at about a 5.75 grade reading level, and none of it contained dangerous information. This shows that drafting and answering FAQs can be delegated, but the material still needs clinician review.
A question-answer chatbot for cataract education tested with 18 patients was rated acceptable (mean SUS 78.6/100), although the sample was small.

COMT job descriptions say the technologist answers patient questions with information as directed by the provider and supports patients and families in person in the clinic. That keeps a human doing the in-person teaching and following the provider's direction.

Prophix markets autonomous FP&A agents, launched in September 2025, including a budgeting agent that updates plans from plain-language input and a reporting agent that writes variance commentary. A reviewer says their accuracy in production is still unproven.

Agentic marketing-budget tools, such as Domo's Budget Allocation agent, analyze channel and campaign performance and reallocate spend using data from BigQuery, Snowflake and Salesforce. The search found no tool aimed specifically at PR or communications budgets.

Agents for budget variance tracking can flag overspends and draft explanations automatically. Final approval of spending priorities and negotiations over agency retainers stay with managers, and this needs no physical presence.

AI warehouse-design simulators exist and handle layout and planning work. GreyOrange's GreyMatter Foundry, launched in April 2026, combines flow design, technology sizing and layout planning, and includes a conversational AI design assistant. Addverb's tool generates 2D layouts from dimensions and storage needs. An agent with tool use could run sub-steps like these, along with capacity analysis, equipment comparisons and ROI work.

No AI tool was found that handles a whole facility expansion end to end. Current tools cover the concept and simulation stages. Site assessment, capital approval, vendor negotiation and overseeing implementation still need humans, and some of that work is physical, such as site walks and supervising construction and installation.

Structural changes to buildings usually need plans signed or sealed by a licensed engineer or architect before a permit is issued. That signature falls to outside licensed professionals, not to the logistics manager, so it limits only the structural part of the task.

BLS says these technicians help mechanical engineers design, develop, test and manufacture devices. Their listed duties include setting up and running tests on units and their parts, logging the results, reviewing drawings and building mechanical parts. Testing and building are hands-on work.

MecAgent V2 is a commercial agent that runs inside SolidWorks. The vendor says it can turn text into CAD, convert models to drawings, build assemblies, check standards and generate bills of materials, including an assembly of about 56 parts built without supervision. These claims are not independently checked, so a human still has to review the output.

Research from 2026 (TOOLCAD, ACL Findings) says a fully autonomous CAD agent that works with real design platforms does not exist yet. CoLab argues that making the geometry is only the first step and the harder engineering work comes after it.

Robotic total stations, which have existed since 1990, use servomotors and a tracking sensor to follow a prism. The operator controls the survey from the prism pole, so the instrument operator is no longer needed. Even so, a person still has to carry the pole and hold it plumb over each point. That work is physical and a software-only AI agent cannot do it.

The Leica iCON robot 50 is sold for one-person surveys run from a field controller mounted on the prism pole at the point being positioned. Setting up and holding the rod still takes a human in the field.

The FDA has cleared AI-based computerized cognitive screening tools such as CognICA, a 5-minute iPad test for early dementia, and Cognivue. These screen for impairment. They do not diagnose CNS disease or treat it.
Georgia rules treat neuropsychological testing and diagnostic opinions on organic brain disorders as the practice of psychology, and unlicensed people may not provide them.
According to AACN, most U.S. states restrict who may use psychological and neuropsychological tests, and some limit them to licensed clinical psychologists, for example Illinois.

A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools found that Khanmigo can tutor students on its own during remedial math sessions. Gains were modest, about 0.06 to 0.08 SD per year. Students used it little, and the authors say low engagement was the main limit.

When Khanmigo asked guiding questions instead of giving answers, students often stopped using it. This suggests that a human's in-person presence and motivation still matter, especially for young children.
Under ESSA/Title I, paraprofessionals must work under a certified teacher's supervision. No licence is needed to tutor, so this rule would not stop an agent from doing the tutoring.

SignNow sells templated DJ contracts covering performance, payment and scheduling. It presents electronic signatures as legally recognized under ESIGN/UETA (vendor claim), so no wet-ink or in-person step is needed.
Cal.com's DJ booking workflow guide says a booking tool can trigger a DJ contract template sent through DocuSign or a similar e-signature service when a booking is made.
AI drafting agents and generators produce service agreements from a plain-language description or a structured set of questions, with Word/PDF export (vendor claims, not independently tested).

Focusing moving lights is done on the lighting console using stored position and focus palettes. Software such as FocusTrack helps check and touch up focus cue by cue, but a human programmer runs it. The search found no fully automatic focus feature in current consoles.

Rigging and electrical work in many venues must be done or supervised by ETCP-certified people, under venue rules and IATSE agreements. This is an industry and union requirement, not a general legal licence, and it assumes human hands-on work.
ETCP certifies Riggers and Entertainment Electricians as experienced practitioners of the physical work: hanging, cabling and powering fixtures.

Histotechnology training is mostly hands-on bench practice (microtomy, embedding, frozen sectioning, staining), plus about 10 hours of lectures a week in the first months. That puts most of the teaching at the physical bench.

A 2025 review sees large language models and multimodal AI personalizing pathology education and cutting content-development work, but with ongoing human oversight so AI supports educators instead of replacing them.
Curricula combine lectures, tutorial demonstrations and rotations through hospital labs, so demonstrating techniques and coaching in person stay central.

Fire departments use NFPA 1582 to require medical and physical fitness exams for firefighters. The standard covers aerobic capacity, strength and endurance, and a physician must confirm that the person can do essential tasks such as rescue. This shows the task is physical work done in person by certified people.

Departments give the NFPA 1582 medical exam at hire and then every year. A physician reports whether each firefighter is fit to do the job's essential physical tasks, so a certified human is held responsible for doing the work.

The fitness requirements set by the standard (grip and limb strength, muscular endurance) reflect the main parts of a rescue: carrying victims, forcing entry and getting people out of water. An agent that works only through software cannot do these things.

Crime scene protocols say the first officer gives the investigator taking control a detailed briefing at the scene and records the handover. The investigator asks what was done and what changed. This is a face-to-face exchange inside a secured scene.
