Department policy has the securing officer go over the scene and events with the detective once the detective arrives, while making sure no one touches the physical evidence. This requires being physically present and moving carefully around evidence.

Axon Draft One turns body-camera audio into draft reports, but officers must review and sign each one. Some deployments leave out felonies and arrests, so AI only helps with documentation and does not replace the briefing itself.

Casino AI surveillance systems (EagleSight, Dallmeier, Xsen) already flag past-posting, bet capping, pinching and dealer payout errors. This takes over part of the cheat-spotting work but does not keep the supervisor's own knowledge current; that still needs a human.
At G2E in October 2026, operators such as MGM and Resorts World were using AI and RFID table-game monitoring alongside human staff, not instead of them.

Game-protection training (card counting, past-posting, collusion, chip fraud) is something the human learns, and it sits alongside surveillance training. An AI can gather research and write briefings, but the familiarity has to stay with the licensed floor supervisor.

Casino accounting systems such as Konami SYNKROS and G+D CashView already automate revenue audit and drop/count reconciliation. One case study says revenue audit went from 4-5 days behind to 24 hours, so the reconciliation sub-steps can be done by software.

Under NIGC MICS (25 CFR 543.17), drop and count must be supervised by an agent with equal or greater authority, and results must be documented. This keeps a human supervisor accountable for the final review and sign-off.
Nevada MICS require supervisors to authorize and document transfers and other accounting steps. Initials do not count as a valid signature, so a named human must attest to the records.

Apaleo and THE FLAG use an agentic AI 'Trace Agent' in live hotel operations. It reads reservation comments and creates about 30 housekeeping tasks a day without a person, so routine task creation and dispatch can already be handed to an agent.

Housekeeping tools such as HelloShift learn from past room assignments to assign cleaners automatically, by zone or floor and with checkouts first. Supervisors still handle on-floor problems and changes in real time.

Salon scheduling software matches stylists to services, checks real-time availability and notifies stylists. This covers the scheduling side of coordinating stylists but not in-person direction, coaching or quality checks.

GovGuard (a Y Combinator company) says its AI agents search years of city records, flag sensitive information for redaction and draft response letters for staff to review. This suggests humans still review responses before they go out.
Datagrid describes AI agents that handle public records requests end to end: intake, search across systems, redaction, deadline tracking and updates to requesters.

A village ordinance names the clerk-treasurer as records access officer, who must grant or deny requests within five business days and certify true copies or that no record was found after a diligent search.

Voice and chat AI agents in 2026 take first notice of loss, check coverage, send out assessors or contractors and update claimants. Vendors report that 45–65% of interactions are resolved without a human, and that agents hand coverage disputes back to people.
In April 2026 Hippo rolled out Clara, an AI voice agent for first notice of loss. Hippo expects more than 70% of homeowners claims to be filed digitally as a result.

Staff without an insurance licence may give routine, clerical and claims-processing help. They may not sell, negotiate or advise, so giving limited claim instructions does not usually require a licensed human.

Policy administration workflows already sort each termination by type (client-requested, insurer-initiated, non-payment, cooling-off), produce the matching communications and update the policy record at each step. This is the core of notifying the parties involved.

InsuredMine, an agency CRM, has cancellation workflow automation that tags cancelled policies with a cancellation date and sends notifications by email, text or task. Its knowledge-base page is vendor release notes, not an independent source.

A vendor guide from 2026 (marketing material, with no cancellation-specific metrics) says AI agents handle policy servicing: they process policy changes and deliver documents through software alone, with no physical step. The notices to the agent and accounting are internal messages; statutory cancellation notices go to the insured, so no licensed human signature is needed.

OSHA's logging standard 29 CFR 1910.266 has its own training section. As I understand it, that section requires a qualified person to train workers, including on-the-job, and to certify the training. My searches showed the standard has a training section but did not return its text, so this detail is my reading and is not quoted here.

OSHA's eTool checklists for chain saws and felling are keyed to 1910.266(e) and (h). They cover physical field practices such as planning a retreat path while the tree falls, which are taught at the work site.

Digital forestry training exists as VR hazard-recognition simulators (for example Mills Skills VR, Scion and harvester simulators). I found no evidence of generative AI or an autonomous agent delivering hands-on felling or machine-operation training.

Landus SkyScout flies fixed-wing aircraft and drones over fields every 12 days and uses AI to flag low emergence, weed pressure, stress, nutrient deficiency and disease. Landus agronomists review each scan before it becomes a recommendation, so a human still makes the decision.

In Taranis-style scouting, drone operators collect leaf-level images in the field. The AI detects weeds, disease and insects and suggests actions, but the farmer or agronomist makes the in-season management decision.
A 2024 GRDC paper calls autonomous agronomy (drone-in-a-box scouting, language-model recommendations) emerging but not yet established, and agronomists remain central to the work.

Livestock transport management systems such as Tracx and AMCS Livestock Planner already schedule, dispatch and re-plan loads, track species welfare transit limits, and take transport requests through portals. That means the 'arrange for transport' part can be handled digitally.

Hauling livestock requires a human driver working under FMCSA hours-of-service rules, with agricultural exemptions. Loading animals, equipment and feed and driving them to work sites are physical jobs an agent without a body cannot do. The rules govern the drivers, so they do not require a human to make the arrangements.

Dispatch tools for livestock and feed haulers include driver apps, GPS tracking and ETA notifications. An agent with access could book carriers and coordinate logistics, but farm supervisors often move supplies themselves on informal or offline systems.

Agents for food and supply-chain buying (Instacart's agentic checkout, Infios supply-chain agents) already handle cart building and purchase orders within set rules. Agents built specifically for buying farm supplies are mostly still forecasts.

Under federal rules, only certified applicators or people they directly supervise may buy restricted-use pesticides, and dealers may not sell them to anyone uncertified. So insecticide purchases often need a licensed human buyer.
Some states go further. Kansas requires private applicator certification to buy restricted-use pesticides, and Wisconsin allows no supervisory exemptions.

FieldClock and similar farm labor tools already handle crew scheduling, attendance and piecework tracking. One review notes that FieldClock's schedule shows what work needs doing but not which workers are assigned, so the supervisor still has to make the assignments.
Toolhouse markets an AI agent that reviews harvest schedules and flags crew or equipment conflicts. This shows agents can take on key sub-steps, although the vendor shows no independent results.

Agriculture workforce software generates schedules from worker availability and skills and says it adjusts them for weather and crop cycles. Real crew and equipment availability is still often known only informally on the farm, which limits what an agent can reach.

A Department of Labor seasonal job posting for this occupation (SOC 45-2092) lists 'clean work areas and maintain grounds and landscaping' among duties that are manual, done with hand tools, and include moving pots and flats of up to 50 lb.

O*NET describes the occupation as manual planting, cultivating and harvesting with hand tools. It points to a separate occupation, Landscaping and Groundskeeping Workers, for grounds upkeep. Both are physical, on-site work.

Autonomous commercial mowers such as the Husqvarna Automower 560 EPOS (2026) are robots, which fall outside the reference technology. A software agent could at most schedule or monitor them, which is a negligible share of the task.

In Wageningen's Autonomous Greenhouse Challenge, teams' AI algorithms set climate setpoints remotely, and a climate and irrigation process computer ran the actuators. In the cherry tomato trial, all AI-supported teams outperformed a greenhouse run by human growers. This shows setpoint control can be delegated where the greenhouse already has automated actuators.

Commercial controllers such as GrowDirector advertise AI software that runs climate control, irrigation/fertigation and EC/pH dosing through dry-contact relays, with app-based monitoring and control. This is vendor marketing, not independent performance data.

Cloud systems such as Click2Cloud's Greenhouse Pilot say they automate climate, humidity, lighting and irrigation for small growers. But for a crop laborer, the task also includes manually opening vents, adjusting valves and moving hoses, which needs a person on site.

Farm management software such as Croptracker already records spray applications by block, tracks chemical inventory and costs, and logs harvest yields by block and commodity. An agent could fill in these records and analyse them from data a worker provides.

Federal rules for restricted-use pesticides (7 CFR 110) require the certified private applicator to keep a record within 14 days. The record covers product, EPA registration number, quantity, date and location. The applicator is responsible for the record, but the law does not require a human to physically write it.

The source data, such as what was sprayed, how much, where and what was harvested, comes from physical field work and observation. A human or a sensor still has to capture it before an agent can record it.

Machine-vision plant grading exists only as dedicated machines that have cameras and sorting mechanics, such as Carnegie Mellon's strawberry plant grader and the patented bin-to-bin sorter. A software-only agent has no body to handle plants or check bud ties in the field.

Commercial AI vision systems like Aris grade potted plants on health, size, shape, colour and defects. They need fixed camera hardware installed in the facility, so an agent could at most review images a human or a machine has already captured.

Human grading of nursery seedlings is subjective, with no consensus on about 1 in 4 trees. This suggests AI could help as a second opinion on photos, but a person still has to do the physical inspection.

Autonomous nursery work is done by dedicated robots, not software agents. The first commercial machine went to a Swedish nursery in late 2025 and is doing border spraying in 2026; that spraying was previously done by hand. A software-only AI agent cannot do this physical work.
Robotic weeding for nursery seedling beds, such as the University of Idaho prototype, is still years from commercial production. Planting, weeding and pruning remain hands-on work done with tools.

Restricted-use pesticides may only be applied by a certified applicator or someone under their direct supervision. Routine planting, watering, weeding and pruning need no licence, so this applies only to part of the spraying.
Maintaining traps is hands-on work. Traps are boiled, dyed and waxed, then the dog and pan notch are filed down. Baseplates, springs, chains and swivels are inspected and repaired by hand.
Lobstermen do off-season 'gear work' on their traps: they build new ones, replace worn parts and fix doors, bait bags and broken laths. All of this is physical work on the traps.

Regulations set some trap features, such as breakaway or bio-vent panels that corrode open. They do not require a licensed person to do or sign off on repairs. The software-only part is limited to looking up specs or rules and ordering parts.

Kongsberg and Viam's Sonar AI works with Simrad fishing sonars such as the SY60. It watches sonar data streams on its own, detects fish automatically, alerts captains and crews when targets appear, and logs fishing activity.

Furuno commercial sonars (FSV-85 Mk2, CSH10) can lock onto a school and track it automatically, and can estimate a school's size and density. A human usually has to pick the target first, and the crew still steers the vessel and runs the equipment on board.
AI species classification from echosounder data is still at the research stage. AZTI's tool reaches about 63.5-80% accuracy on pelagic schools, so a human still has to check what it finds.

USDA APHIS Wildlife Services' damage control and disease work is done in the field: trapping, sampling wild birds for avian influenza and other surveillance, and sending people to sites within 48 hours. The 2005 directive bases this work on the Act of March 2, 1931.
Field deployments for disease response add up to thousands of person-days, such as 1400 deployed days for HPAI and over 2000 for ASF. That work needs a person physically present and handling animals.

Software tools like ClassifyMe and TrapTagger already classify camera-trap images, filter out empty frames and write detection reports. This covers only the digital data-processing part of the research work.
Deckhands wash vessel decks by hand with high-pressure hoses and brushes, using marine soap to remove mud and biofouling. This is physical work done on board.
Processing surfaces and equipment on fishing vessels have to be cleaned and sanitized every day, and ice holds after each fishing period. This means physically handling the equipment on the boat.
OSHA treats deck housekeeping and the safe handling of cleaning chemicals as hands-on crew practices for preventing injuries. It describes no software role in doing the cleaning.

Vendor material for 2026 describes procurement AI agents that find a supply shortfall, pick pre-approved vendors, draft purchase orders and send them for approval without step-by-step human input. These are vendor examples, not studies of real deployments.

Maritime software such as Kongsberg K-Fleet Provision and its C-Purchase and C-Spares modules already handles vessel provision ordering, inventory and stock control, and syncs order data between ship and shore.

Marine procurement software such as DNV ShipManager is built to stop over-ordering and stock-outs of spares and stores. Deciding which gear is worn and needs replacing still means someone has to inspect it on board.
